LHCb data from 2010, the effective lifetime for the $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ decay has been measured. While the conventional stance holds that table instances must adhere to all imposed functional dependencies, it is equally significant to formulate theories for handling instances that violate certain dependencies. Concerning missing values, we do not presuppose their existence; rather, a missing value is considered to exist only if it can be inferred from the table's functional dependencies.

We present a formal framework where each table tuple is assigned one of four truth values: true, false, inconsistent, or unknown. We demonstrate that this framework facilitates the study of critical issues such as consistent query answering, table merging, and data cleaning. Specifically, we examine the computational complexities of these problems across various scenarios, considering both the absence and presence of partial and full relational schemas. Furthermore, we offer positive results by characterizing problems through their parameterized complexity.

We demonstrate that the score-driven approach is ideal for tracking the evolution of time-varying parameters, offering the necessary flexibility to handle count data with complex nonlinear dynamics and structural breaks. Designed for object manipulation, this approach enables the repetition of a demonstrated task on new instances within the same category by optimizing for a pose whose descriptor matches the observed demonstration. NDFs are trained in a self-supervised manner through a 3D-to-2D process that requires only Dense Description Networks (DDN2D) to be demonstrated. Unlike traditional 2D-to-2D methods, we utilize 3D demonstrations because multiple 2D images from the same camera position often depict different parts of the object, and conversely, identical object parts may appear in images captured from vastly different locations. To address the challenge of scaling to arbitrary scenes and object sizes, our 3D representation is compact and adaptive. This approach significantly reduces demonstration requirements: we need demonstrate only a single image per part (scaling with the number of parts rather than total points) and a single 3D pose (translating to one pan motion), even in scenes with unknown backgrounds and at scales differing from training data. This compact representation is efficient, allowing the optimization of poses for novel objects a thousand times faster than optimizing point clouds. Furthermore, this optimization can be performed on modern GPUs in real-time. We validated NDFs using both synthetic and real-world data, showing that despite being a recent advancement over our prior 2D descriptor representation, the method dramatically lowers demonstration burdens. For the TAMP framework to effectively plan for new objects, the optimization time must be negligible compared to planning and execution; our results confirm that optimizing poses from NDFs is easily achievable in real-time. Existing literature is generally categorized into two approaches based on the use of intermediate cues: direct methods and two-stage pipelines. In the two-stage pipeline, CNNs first predict a 3D position (including depth and orientation) in image coordinates in the first stage, which then serves as a key input for the second stage to estimate depth and full pose in 3D space. However, current pipelines often rely on standard 2D super-resolution techniques to recover the3D image. These traditional methods are computationally expensive and, more critically, fail to fully exploit the structural characteristics of the 3D image. This work introduces a two-stage pipeline for estimating 3D images and object instances by integrating advanced 2D super-resolution techniques. Unlike prior art, our proposed 3D image upsampling network (3DUI-NET) accounts for the independent nature of object instances within 3D images. Additionally, we offer a revised version of the SYBOPose benchmark to facilitate the evaluation and comparison of 3D image estimation methods. Experimental results indicate that the 3DUI-NET significantly surpasses current 2D upsamplers in image-based 3D estimation while requiring approximately 20 times fewer parameters and 30 times less training time. The source code and models are publicly available at: https://github.com/zhengjiajun/3DUI-NET.

Our implementation utilizes the Proximal Alternating Linearized Sensing approach by `GrohsSchoberl14` to resolve these estimates. The software includes a `add_node` function, which dynamically adds a new node to an existing graph and calculates its specific precision matrix. Furthermore, the library features a `add_edge` function that accommodated two scenarios: (1) adding an edge to a graph where both connected nodes already exist, and (2) inserting a directed edge from a new node into a graph. To ensure the graph remains undirected, the latter scenario automatically adds a reverse edge. GGLasso also offers `remove_node` and `remove_edge` functions for deleting nodes and edges, respectively, from the graph. Additionally, our software incorporates detection mechanisms for disconnected components and isolated nodes within the graph. The implementation is built upon the `graphene` package by `Hunter17` to manage graph-related operations. The codebase is fully open-source, allowing users to access all source files, and comes with comprehensive examples and tutorials. We validated our implementation against a range of synthetic and real-world scenarios. Specifically, for real data, we recovered a 3-node graph from gene expression matrices of breast cancer patients and reconstructed a directed 4-node graph using eye movement data from two participants in a visual search experiment. For the undirected case, we estimated a 200-node graph from brain imaging data collected from two individuals and a 500-node graph from gene expression data of two individuals from two distinct species. The software is released under the permissive MIT license. GGLasso is accessible via `pip install GGLasso` or by downloading it directly from the GitHub repository at https://github.com/BehnamShakibi/GGLasso.

By examining extensive families of four-dimensional Type IIB $\mathcal{N}=2$ effective field theories, we identify potential generalized global symmetries and demonstrate how they are circumvented. A key component in these theories involves generalized $\theta$-terms, which establish non-linear interactions between axion fields and gauge field strength terms quadratic in topology, thereby disrupting a significant portion of global symmetries. Furthermore, assuming the presence of charged states can break any remaining residual symmetries. However, we show that generalized $\theta$-terms induce a generalized Witten effect, implying that the charged state spectrum forms an infinitely populated lattice. We also demonstrate that this lattice arises from the monodromy transformation acting on the moduli space boundary where the effective theory is defined. While this lattice does not constitute a genuine global symmetry group, it obstructs the application of the no global symmetries theorem, necessitating a revised framework for charged state spectra in $\mathcal{N}=2$ EFTs. The same argument applies to $\mathcal{N}=2$ supergravity theories derived from Type II string theory, Calabi-Yau threefolds, F-theory on Kähler surfaces, and torus compactifications of six-dimensional $\mathcal{N}=(1,0)$ superconformal field theories. Additionally, generalized $\theta$-terms imply a generalized Dyson sphere effect; thus, if no charged states exist, any generalized $\mathbb{Z}$ global symmetry is violated. This mechanism involves non-linear axion self-interactions in the Lagrangian that are incompatible with generalized $\mathbb{Z}$ global symmetries, and this effect arises from moduli space monodromies akin to the charged state lattice. Ultimately, the generalized Witten effect and the generalized Dyson sphere effect combine to prove that no global symmetries exist in the $\mathcal{N}=2$ EFTs under consideration, unless the state spectrum contains an infinitely populated lattice. If such a lattice is present, it is compatible with the existence of a conformal point in the IR limit, as this defines a genuine global symmetry group. Consequently, we outline the steps required to generalize the no global symmetries theorem to $\mathcal{N}=2$ EFTs and present a framework for analyzing global symmetries in conformal $\mathcal{N}=2$ theories. acts as a crucial testing ground for fundamental quantum mechanics and various applications, including metrology and on-chip communication. Quantum nonlinear circuits, however face limitations imposed by the discrete nature of their harmonic oscillators. This study introduces a "continuous" analog of the Duffing Hamiltonian by coupling two modes to a thermal bath engineered to facilitate coherent communication among $N$-phonon states. We demonstrate that, despite the challenge of navigating a non-Hamiltonian analog landscape, a Hamiltonian dynamics emerges within an $M$-phonon subspace ($M \le N$) for a regime of interest defined by specific bath parameters. This effective Hamiltonian enables the conversion of multi-phonon states into photon-like states, facilitating their detection through standard homodyne measurement techniques. Furthermore, we outline a quantitative method to determine the boundaries of this effective Hamiltonian dynamics and outline a protocol to explicitly construct the apparatus state required to yield the simplified measurement procedure. These findings provide a systematic methodology to identify regimes where a complex, open-system description yields a Hamiltonian effective in a targeted state space, ultimately allowing for experimental verification via straightforward measurement schemes. This methodology is broadly applicable to analyze proposals involving the interaction of multiple modes with engineered environments.

Using a nearest-neighbour tight-binding model with horizontal and vertical hopping, we identify two non-equivalent Dirac cones within the first Brillouin zone along a high-symmetry trajectory. These cones can be manipulated through various Hamiltonian perturbations that break lattice symmetries; initially, we introduce distinct onsite potentials, which cause the Dirac cones to evolve into semi-Dirac cones and nodal lines along high-symmetry paths. Subsequently, we apply hopping term dimerization, observing the migration of Dirac cones across the first Brillouin zone along quasi-hyperbolic trajectories. Additionally, we outline a feasible experimental realization involving CO atoms adsorbed on a Cu(111) surface. This work offers a simple yet effective framework for understanding symmetry-based Dirac cones in 2D lattice models and how they can be shifted or transformed into other topological defects through relatively straightforward local or non-local symmetries. These findings have potential applications in lattice engineering and the design of materials with novel properties. (This contribution is part of the EMAP 2020 virtual proceedings).

**Background and Motivation**

MRI data is increasingly being used for brain research across diverse applications, including clinical diagnostics and publications. This trend necessitates robust quality control (QC) to ensure data reliability. While leveraging institutional data can strengthen models and reduce bias, a critical challenge in deep learning for MRI QC is the poor generalization of models trained on data from a single institution when applied to institutions with different scanners, software, and protocols. This paper investigates the generalization of learning methods across institutions in the context of MRI QC. We compare three approaches trained on data from both institutions against a baseline trained solely on one institution's data. Our results indicate that utilizing data from multiple institutions reduces bias and enhances the generalization of models across different institutions.

All established bounds are optimal up to universal multiplicative constants. Numerical illustrations accompany several inequalities to further demonstrate their tightness. The proposed framework also facilitates the derivation of analogous results on other product spaces. Our approach for SRP inequalities utilizes the multi-parameter Brascamp–Lieb inequalities on the discrete cube, a tool of independent interest that generalizes classical results such as the Harris inequality, the Poincaré inequality, and the matrix Chebychev inequality. For both random vectors with SCP and SRP, we provide detailed examinations of specific matrix-valued functions, offering comparisons with existing literature and presenting new findings. In the case of stochastic matrices, our bounds are shown to be sharp up to universal constants. The associated computations are exceptionally intricate; indeed, these bounds represent the most stringent non-trivial estimates known for random vectors on the discrete cube.

of patient-donor incompatibility, a challenge that has intensified due to the growing shortage of donors and spurred the creation of desensitization methods. However, incompatible transplants carry higher risks of rejection, infection, cancer, and graft loss compared to compatible ones. This study investigates the optimal acceptance strategies for potentially incompatible kidneys tailored to individual patients with end-stage kidney disease. To model the impact of incompatibility, we introduce a Markov Decision Process (MDP) framework that treats compatibility as an explicit state variable. Although this results in a higher-dimensional model that complicates analysis, we derive structural properties—specifically control limit-type optimal policies—that are straightforward to calculate and apply. Numerical simulations demonstrate how the optimal policy behaves across varying mismatch levels and underscore the necessity of integrating incompatibility status directly into acceptance decisions, particularly when desensitization therapy is available. Although these findings are theoretical, they offer actionable guidance for clinicians managing the increasing pool of incompatible kidneys amid ongoing desensitization advancements. Decisions regarding the acceptance of potentially incompatible organs are increasingly relevant; therefore, our results can be readily adapted to reflect actual patient and donor characteristics. Although we focused on incompatibility arising from ABO blood type mismatches, the model and derived properties are universally applicable to any source of incompatibility, whether binary (e.g., HLA matching scores) or more complex. Ultimately, the simplicity of the proposed model enables easy adaptation to other incompatibility metrics, such as HLA matching scores, and accommodability extensions can address multiple sources of mismatch or concurrent competing priorities. Although we assumed immediate treatment upon acceptance, the framework can also be extended to evaluate "testing and waiting" strategies, where the recipient's blood is typed and sent to the allocation network before organ arrival. Finally, while we focused on the initial acceptance decision, the framework is likewise suitable for analyzing post-transplant desensitization policies.

By employing a mathematical formulation, we reveal the implicit structural assumptions inherent in adopting this model. Specifically, we demonstrate that Markovian assumptions provide a clear theoretical framework for understanding embedding formation, particularly regarding the capture of frequentist synonyms. We provide a mathematical proof of the model's efficacy in learning these relationships and support our findings with numerical experiments. Our contributions advance the field theoretically, moving beyond empirical observations to establish how embeddings are genuinely learned. This approach contrasts with prior efforts that merely explained why embeddings are useful heuristics for specific tasks; instead, we detail the precise mechanism of embedding learning. To ensure clarity and avoid ambiguity often found in engineering contexts, all equations are derived explicitly throughout this study. Additionally, we prove that the Markovian assumption represents the simplest possible framework for learning embeddings, a conclusion reinforced by numerical experiments showing that more complex models do not necessarily yield better outcomes. Finally, our proposed generalized model serves as a blueprint for developing advanced models capable of capturing explicit semantic relationships. Nevertheless, in the fundamental context of multiplayer general-sum games, current algorithms necessitate an exponential number of samples relative to the player count to learn rationalizable equilibria under bandit feedback. This paper introduces the first family of efficient learning algorithms for rationalizable Correlated Equilibria and Rationalizable Nash Equilibria. Specifically, in an auxiliary game derived from the original, we can learn a rationalizable correlated equilibrium in a sample complexity polynomial in both the dimension of actions and the number of players. Furthermore, in scenarios where a Nash equilibrium is guaranteed to exist, our efforts to learn the corresponding strategies and their mixed strategies in this auxiliary game enable the efficient acquisition of rationalizable Nash equilibria. To achieve this, the proposed method utilizes $O(\log (n \cdot |A|))$ samples for a multiplayer general-sum game with $n$ players and action space size $|A|$. To underscore the significance of this finding, we highlight that for a general-class multiplayer general-sum game, any algorithm learning a $\epsilon$-rationalizable Nash Equilibrium requires a sample complexity of $\tilde{\Omega}(\frac{|A|^2}{\epsilon})$, which exceeds the quadratic complexity in $\epsilon$ observed in the Nash equilibrium sample complexity of bimatrix games. Additionally, regarding the efficient learning of rationalizable equilibria in bimatrix games, we establish a lower bound of $\tilde{\Omega}(\sqrt{|A|})$ for the sample complexity required by algorithms learning $\epsilon$-rationalizable Nash Equilibria; this bound applies even to pure Nash equilibria within zero-sum games. These lower bounds surpass those found in existing literature, which focus on scenarios where the Nash equilibrium is embedded within a subgame of a larger game and assume knowledge of this equilibrium. To accomplish this, we introduce a novel analysis technique for rationalizability sample complexity that extends beyond the standard support size lower bound. This approach encompasses two key innovations: (1) utilizing a specific type of conditional lower bound, and (2) employing a specific analytical framework for rationalizable equilibrium sample complexity that exceeds the quadratic sample complexity inherent in the standard support size lower bound. A distinctive feature of both the upper and lower bounds for rationalizable equilibria in bimatrix games is the ability to precisely determine the exact coefficients within the complexity expressions. The network structure follows an Erdős–Rényi random graph, but susceptible individuals adjacent to infectious nodes may sever or rewire these links during the epidemic. We derive large-population limits that establish convergence for the initial branching process phase and, under the assumption of a major outbreak, for the subsequent epidemic phase, which approaches a deterministic model equivalent to a specific pair approximation. While classical experience replay enables agents to retain knowledge by reusing past observations, its uniform sampling strategy treats all data points equally, neglecting their varying significance. To address this, we introduce a general Variance Reduction-based Experience Replay (VRER) framework that selectively prioritizes the most relevant samples to refine policy gradient estimates. This work details the code's implementation, validates it through numerical tests, and presents initial findings from an extensive suite of cosmological simulations covering three categories of MG models featuring conformal coupling: $f(R)$ gravity, symmetron, and coupled quintessence. Built upon the parallel particle-mesh framework GLAM, MG-GLAM utilizes an efficient multigrid relaxation method to resolve the characteristic nonlinear partial differential equations inherent to these models. Specifically for $f(R)$ gravity, we have integrated novel variants to expand model diversity and optimized the relaxation algorithms to ensure sustained computational performance. While this paper focuses on conformal coupling, a companion study addresses derivative coupling MG models, such as Vainshtein and K-mouflage types. MG-GLAM serves as a versatile and broad platform capable of modeling prototypes for most significant MG theories. The code is highly optimized, achieving a speedup exceeding one hundred times that of previous $N$-body codes while maintaining high accuracy in predicting the matter power spectrum and dark matter halo abundance. Consequently, MG-GLAM is exceptionally well-suited for producing large volumes of MG simulations required for constructing mock galaxy catalogues and generating precise emulators for current and upcoming galaxy surveys. MG-GLAM is now available for public download.

These findings generalize to GFFs with arbitrary distributed boundary conditions. Furthermore, this relaxed definition of conformal equivalence provides a more natural framework for defining imaginary surfaces within conformal field theory.

Within a linearized framework, capturing heat release fluctuations is essential for studying thermoacoustic instabilities and flame noise. Distinct from prior work, this study employs an active flame approach, which incorporates heat release oscillations induced by acoustic fluctuations. Implementing this approach linearly requires linearizing a combustion model; however, linearizing Large Eddy Simulation (LES) and Direct Numerical Simulation (DNS) models creates closure issues, rendering them difficult to apply in this context. Conversely, Reynolds-averaged Navier Stokes (RANS) models effectively avoid these problems, making them ideal for this application. These RANS models were linearized around the temporal mean flow of the turbulent jet, which was derived using LES. An a priori analysis identified the linearized RANS-Eddy Break Up (EBU) model as yielding the most accurate LES-derived mean flow. Consequently, this model was selected to linearly model a turbulent methane-air jet experimentally investigated by Schuller et al. The linearized operator was applied to experimental data to calculate the linearized flame response. These responses were then compared against the linearized EBU model's predictions using experimental LES mean flows, demonstrating strong agreement. Finally, the linearized operator was employed to investigate the influence of Mach number on the subsonic flame response. Linearized simulations were performed across a range of Mach numbers to replicate the experimental setup, and their results were compared with actual experimental data, again showing good agreement. The excellent concordance between the experimental LES mean flows, real-world experiments, and linearized simulations underscores the value of this approach for analyzing experimental data. Furthermore, this method offers a cost-effective means of investigating subsonic and supersonic reacting flows and their reactions to acoustic actuation.

, nonlocal extension of Einstein's gravitational theory, modeled after the analogy with nonlocal electrodynamics in media. Within this framework, historical dependence is introduced through a constitutive relation that utilizes a causal kernel, which must ultimately be derived from observational data. This paper aims to reformulate nonlocal gravity so that the nonlocal components of the constitutive relation directly link measurable quantities, mirroring the approach found in nonlocal electrodynamics. The derived constitutive relation aligns with a recent proposal by Puetzfeld, Obukhov, and Hehl [25]. Utilizing this updated constitutive relation for NLG, it is demonstrated that de Sitter spacetime does not constitute a valid solution. Furthermore, applying this framework to weak-field and slow-motion approximations yields a constitutive relation that agrees with the previously established result by Obukhov and Puetzfeld [20]. However, a new finding emerges when adopting the constitutive relation from [25]: the specific form of the Boltzmann-GG profile in nonlocal gravity is no longer determined solely by the dark energy parameter $\lambda$, as was the case with the constitutive relation from [18]. Instead, according to [25], the relationship is governed by the equation $f(\phi)=\exp\left(-\frac{|\phi|}{\lambda}\right)$, where $\phi = \sqrt{8\pi G}\,\varphi$ and $\varphi$ denotes the scalar potential. This indicates that the influence of finite light speed in NLG on the Boltzmann-GG profile is minimal. Consequently, both constitutive relations can coexist in NLG because they rely on fundamentally different approximations. The constitutive relation from [25] is derived without such approximations, whereas the one from [18] was obtained under the assumption of weak fields and slow motions. Ultimately, the constitutive relation from [25] can be further justified as it yields the same Boltzmann-GG profile identified in [18] within the specified approximation context.

Applying this approach to GWAS data for 18 human traits—including red and platelet cell metrics, glucose and lipid levels, height, BMI, and Crohn's disease—we assessed the relevance of 450 genomic annotations across over a hundred tissues and cell lines, covering protein-coding genes, enhancers, and DNase-I hypersensitive sites. Galactic Centre has been linked to magnetic field amplification following disruptions. This study identifies a similar correlation in a sample of 75 sources from the f4.2m survey. Most of these sources exhibit signs of disk formation, with ellipticities rising as the flux diminishes during the fading phase. These observations align with the prediction that an inflated power-law emission spectrum signifies a strong magnetic field. Furthermore, the source's age determines the maximum achievable ellipticity; after an initial rapid expansion, the disk's growth subsides, resulting in higher final ellipticities for younger sources. However, not all sources reach the threshold necessary to vary their i-band flux variability. This variation arises from an interplay between the viewing angle, the disk's inclination, and its ellipticity. We propose that this entire sequence—variable X-ray brightness, post-disruption ellipticity amplification, and variable i-band variability—is driven by tidal disruptions of main-belt asteroids. These findings offer the first direct evidence of asteroid dynamics within transiting debris disks around white dwarfs. Additionally, the discovered ties between X-ray, optical, and radio emissions in this specific sample suggest that the fastest-evolving sources may originate from a distinct population, potentially involving planetary-sized bodies. (Original abstract authored by A. L. Piro.)

Specifically, when ions are circularly driven at frequencies approaching but remaining below the electron plasma frequency, the electron current acquires an inertia dependent on the Rabi oscillation amplitude. This effect manifests as a nonlinear modification of electron dynamics in face-centered cubic (fcc) potassium crystals, altering the damping of plasmon modes excited by ultrashort circularly polarized femtosecond laser pulses. Furthermore, in nonlinear circularly driven fcc potassium, we observe a shift in the frequency of the lattice's soft mode under THz driving, indicating that we can impart effective mass to phonon branches. This suggests the possibility of generating topological defects, such as knotted phonons, in this system. Using THz circular driving, we can alter the topology of phonon bands in insulators and the effective mass of particles coupled to light in Born-Oppenheimer quantum simulations. Additionally, inertial effects on electrons can be exploited to generate highly correlated states of charge carriers from weakly interacting systems or to produce topological defect dark matter. THz circular polarization offers a novel mechanism for inducing strong correlations and topological defect dark matter, provides a method to change the effective mass of particles in quantum simulations, and allows for the creation of knotted phonons.

We have numerically modeled these rotating objects to determine whether they can sustain nuclear fusion as their energy source, accounting for significant rotational deformation rather than assuming slow rotation. Our results indicate that when angular momentum surpasses a threshold of $J_0=8.85\times 10^{48}{\rm erg}~{\rm s}$, the critical curve splits into two branches representing lower and higher degeneracy. The upper branch behaves like the standard critical curve for sub-stellar objects, while the lower branch forms because, at the same surface temperature, higher interior temperatures in less degenerate sub-stellar objects generate more nuclear energy. This phenomenon cannot be captured by analytic models that assume uniform rotation and spherical shape, as the maximum angular velocity still leads to mass-shedding. Ultimately, our findings demonstrate how observable properties, such as the mass and temperature of the coolest brown dwarfs, are constrained by their angular momentum. The implications of these results for interpreting the spin of brown dwarfs with known angular velocities are also discussed. Numerational data can provide precise critical angular velocities and enhance the understanding of the cooling processes in these objects. Ultimately, this study establishes a foundational framework for analyzing the observability of nuclear burning in rapidly spinning brown dwarfs.

These structures are frequently depicted in a two-tiered layout, where each entity set is shown as a collection of vertices aligned on one of two parallel horizontal lines, and their relationships are illustrated by edges linking corresponding vertices across the lines. A primary goal in creating such visualizations is to reduce edge crossings; however, minimizing crossings is computationally demanding and often yields drawings with so many intersections that they compromise readability. This work examines a recent method for eliminating crossings by splitting vertices, aiming to identify the minimum number of vertices that must be split to achieve a planar representation. We demonstrate that deciding whether a planar drawing is achievable by splitting at most $k$ vertices is fixed parameter tractable with respect to $k$. Furthermore, we show that this problem is also fixed parameter tractable when parameterized by the feedback vertex set size of the graph. Additionally, we address the special case of bipartite outerplanar graphs and present an approximate algorithm for the general case. Throughout these discussions, we include examples that highlight the challenges involved. These results extend prior findings by BergJKMSSS2019 and BartFMSSS2018.

to knot diagrams. It is possible to convert any knot diagram into a trivial unknot diagram through a combination of unknotting operations and Reidemeister moves. These operations hold substantial significance in knot theory, particularly for analyzing knot complexity and invariants. Furthermore, they play a crucial role in fields such as biology, chemistry, and physics, where they help investigate the complex entanglements found in strings, organic molecules, and DNA. This paper introduces a novel unknotting operation known as the diagonal move, applicable to both classical and welded knots. We demonstrate that the crossing change, Delta-move, Sharp-move, Gamma-move, n-gon move, pass move, and 4-move can all be achieved via sequences of diagonal moves. Additionally, we define a distance metric based on the diagonal move and examine its characteristics. These findings highlight that the diagonal move provides a comprehensive framework for understanding various unknotting processes.

This study examines how a team of strategic agents selects among multiple tasks within a stochastic framework, specifically focusing on two tasks with randomly distributed and partially observable difficulties. Operating as a non-cooperative team, these agents act as price-discount consumers who select one of the two available options. These agents are classified into two types, each with a private probability of successfully completing the assigned task. We analyze the equilibrium behaviors for both single-dimensional and multi-dimensional private probabilities. In the latter case, we derive an explicit formula for the equilibrium density function regarding the success probabilities of both agent types and investigate its relationship with the underlying distribution of task difficulties. Furthermore, we offer insights into the impact of a large number of non-cooperative agents on task difficulty distribution and provide recommendations for a representative agent. This work extends our previous analysis, which assumed observable task difficulty and resulted in a unique equilibrium. To our knowledge, this research presents the initial explicit formula for the equilibrium density function when private probabilities are distributed across two dimensions and offers key insights into its implications. Our findings concerning task difficulty and the strategy for representing a mixed-type population are particularly significant, as they contradict the "paradox of choice," demonstrating that an excessive number of options do not necessarily lead to suboptimal outcomes. These results are highly relevant to diverse multi-agent applications, such as load balancing, ride-sharing, trucking, ride-hailing, healthcare, and social media interactions.

Based on collaboration structures, FL is categorized into Horizontal Federated Learning (HFL) and Vertical Federated Learning (VFL). In HFL, entities share identical feature spaces and data samples, whereas in VFL, they share common sample identifiers and collaborate on features. VFL offers a wider application scope and is particularly well-suited for joint model training among large enterprises.

This paper concentrates on VFL, examining potential privacy vulnerabilities within real-world frameworks. We developed and executed two practical privacy attacks: a reverse multiplication attack targeting the logistic regression VFL protocol and a reverse sum attack targeting the XGBoost VFL protocol. Our empirical analysis demonstrates that these attacks are (1) effective, allowing adversaries to extract private training data even when intermediate outputs are encrypted; (2) evasive, as they adhere strictly to protocol specifications and do not degrade the target model's accuracy; and (3) low-effort, requiring minimal prior knowledge of the target participant's data distribution. Furthermore, we show that the information leaked is as potent as the original training data for training alternative classifiers. Finally, we discuss potential countermeasures and their associated challenges, aiming to inspire future research directions. Source code is available here.

To overcome this, Random Fourier Features (RFF) were introduced to approximate kernel functions using randomized Fourier features, enabling scalability. Despite its popularity, RFF has notable limitations: because it samples features from a distribution independent of the training data, it demands a large number of feature dimensions to match the performance of kernelized classifiers, a requirement that scales with dataset size. Consequently, reducing feature dimensions is essential for effective scaling. This paper introduces Pseudo Random Fourier Features (PRFF), a data-dependent kernel approximation technique designed to minimize feature dimensions and enhance predictive performance. The method is evaluated on classification and regression tasks, with comparisons made against RFF, orthogonal random features, and the Nyström approach. Experimental results show that PRFF requires approximately 30% of the feature dimensions of RFF to achieve comparable predictive accuracy. Additionally, PRFF demonstrates faster training and prediction speeds, lower memory usage during training, and superior performance in small-batch predictive scenarios. PRFF also exhibits heightened stability over time compared to both RFF and the Nyström method. Furthermore, we have released a comprehensive codebase alongside a video tutorial to assist researchers in leveraging PRFF. The code is accessible at https://github.com/AmirHaji-88/PRFF.

ultaneous Wireless Information and Power Transfer (SWIPT), designed to enhance communication efficiency in next-generation mobile networks while reducing overall power consumption through green energy sourcing. First, a distinct architecture is proposed where receivers harvest energy from an Access Point (AP) without requiring a signal splitter; in this OFDMA model, specific spectrum portions are allocated for Information Decoding (ID) while others are dedicated to Energy Harvesting (EH). To evaluate performance gains, an optimization problem is formulated to maximize harvested energy in a multi-user single-cell OFDMA downlink while ensuring minimum data rate requirements are met, subsequently solved using Graph Theory to optimize two receiver architectures: Successive Receiver Selection (SRS) and Orthogonal Receiver Allocation (ORA). Subsequently, an enhancement is introduced by applying beamforming techniques to the OFDMAORA SWIPT system to jointly boost energy harvesting and communication rates, solved via Convex Optimization. Finally, in a multi-cell multi-user multi-antenna scenario, a Game Theory approach is employed to solve a common sum-rate maximization problem for two receiver architectures (ORA and ORA without beamforming), considering both external and internal interference to determine the Nash Equilibrium (NE). Simulation results validate the performance improvements achieved across all proposed schemes. Notably, the ofdma-ofdma-ora beamforming configuration offers a significant 300% increase in harvested energy compared to the multi-cell multi-user multi-antenna ofdma-ora architecture. Furthermore, the NE exists and is unique for the ofdma-ora game, whereas it does not exist for the ofdma-srs game.

eliminate malicious phenomena, such as epidemics and misinformation, an area often referred to as network immunization. Traditional methods for assessing attack effectiveness typically rely on macro-level metrics, like the critical percolation probability ($p_c$) and the size of the giant component, often overlooking the micro-level dynamics of node removals, their specific traits, and immediate outcomes. This paper introduces and applies a micro-scale approach to attack analysis. Grounded in network percolation theory, we examine the "avalanche" effect triggered by the removal of a single node from the giant component—a phenomenon where one removal causes a cascade of disconnections that significantly contributes to network fragmentation and immunization beyond the loss of that single node. We specifically analyze the avalanche size, defined as the count of nodes disconnected from the giant component due to one removal. Furthermore, regarding random attacks on Cayley tree networks, we analytically derive the distribution of avalanche sizes throughout the entire attack process, from initiation until the network is fully dismantled and the attack ceases. Our findings reveal that these avalanches follow a power-law distribution with an exponent of $\beta=2$. This result aligns with self-organized criticality observations in Earthquakes and sandpile models, suggesting that Cayley tree networks inherently reside in a critical state during random attacks. Additionally, this power-law behavior implies scale-invariance in natural disasters. Numerical simulations confirm our analytical results and further demonstrate that the average avalanche size grows super-linearly from zero at the onset of attack to a peak, followed by a sub-linear decline to zero as the network is completely destroyed. These insights offer a deeper understanding of network attacks and their impact on immunization, with potential applications extending beyond social and communication domains to include biological, chemical, and physical systems.

This limitation represents a primary barrier to detecting gravitational waves from binary neutron star mergers in both current and future detectors, as it remains independent of arm length and the level of injected squeezing. In this study, we propose a sloshing Sagnac interferometer topology, derived from a Michelson interferometer by optically linking the end mirrors to form an additional cavity. As an evolution of the Michelson architecture, the sloshing-Sagnac interferometer offers a viable topology for upgrading current detectors and for future-generation observatories.

Because the physical dimensions of XL-MIMO arrays are comparable to the distances separating them from user equipments (UEs), the system experiences spatial non-stationarities and distinct visibility regions (VRs). These factors, combined with high UE density and limited pilot resources, make the design of random access (RA) protocols and scheduling algorithms particularly difficult. This paper introduces a joint RA and scheduling approach called the non-overlapping VR XL-MIMO (NOVR-XL) protocol. This method leverages the unique VRs of individual UEs to enhance RA performance and prioritizes scheduling UEs with non-overlapping VRs within the same payload data pilot resource. Simulation results demonstrate that this proposed scheme yields substantial improvements in sum rate compared to conventional RA methods, while also lowering access latency and overall connectivity performance.

sub-millimeter and millimeter wavelengths reveal morphologies characterized by azimuthally or point-symmetric substructures, including spiral arms and localized crescent or spur-like features. While most theoretical efforts to interpret these findings assume that such structures arise from disk-planet interactions, confirmed exoplanet detections in these systems remain scarce. Moreover, certain substructures are anticipated to emerge prior to planet formation, as they are intrinsically linked to the processes driving planet accretion. This study presents a comprehensive overview of the theoretical mechanisms responsible for these substructures and outlines the associated observational predictions. Specifically, we detail the anticipated features in image data and high-resolution spectral data (from millimeter to infrared), covering proposed formation mechanisms for spirals across all wavelength ranges. Additionally, we address other potential formation causes for these substructures, such as magnetohydrodynamic jets, shadowing effects, dead zones, and planet-trapped accretion rings. By compiling recent empirical constraints on physical parameters like opening angles, spacing, and depths from multi-wavelength data, we establish current upper limits on the masses and accretion rates of central forming planets. Finally, we propose a case study to illustrate how high-angular resolution data can guide future detections of directly imaged exoplanets and constrain their physical properties through inverse modeling. These findings are summarized in concluding remarks, accompanied by implications for both current and forthcoming surveys and instruments capable of detecting these substructures in the near future. Recently, Fattoyev et al. developed an Energy Density Functional (EDF) called BigApple, which successfully models a neutron star mass of 2.60 $M_\odot$, aligning well with GW190814 observations. The BigApple functional accurately predicts key properties of finite nuclei, including binding energy per particle, skin thickness, charge radius, single-particle energy, and two-neutron separation energy across various nuclei. Furthermore, calculated nuclear matter quantities such as incompressibility, symmetry energy, and slope parameters at saturation density agree with empirical or experimental data where available. Overall, the BigApple interaction demonstrates robust applicability across both nuclear and nuclear astrophysical systems. Consequently, GW190814 analysis with the BigApple functional suggests that the secondary mass likely corresponds to the most massive neutron star ever detected. Additionally, the BigApple interaction indicates that a 2.60 $M_\odot$ neutron star could exist in the universe. of high-parameter statistical frameworks. While previous research has examined over-parameterized linear models with non-sparse, high-dimensional data, those findings largely rely on the assumption of independent samples. This study investigates linear regression under over-parameterization with dependent time series data. We propose an interpolation-based estimator and establish a theoretical framework for its excess risk across various dependence structures. This approach accommodates infinite-dimensional data without requiring sparsity and unifies the handling of long-memory processes. Furthermore, we bound the risk using integrated covariance and the nondegeneracy of autocorrelation matrices. Our results indicate that convergence rates for short-memory processes match those of independent data, whereas long-memory processes decelerate convergence. Additionally, we provide examples of specific dependent processes applicable to this framework. Finally, simulation results are presented to illustrate the utility of our methodology. To underscore the impact of long-memory effects, we also include an example demonstrating how failure to account for them can lead to biased estimates. A related paper offers lower bounds and optimal estimator constructions for these scenarios. Process long-memory parameters are determined nonparametrically, with optimization complexity independent of dimensionality. The proposed estimator requires no dimensionality reduction and is universally applicable to any stationary time series. Process complexity scales as $O(p_t + t)$, where $p_t$ is the optimal lag and $t$ is the sample size. Our findings generalize prior work on long-memory linear processes with independent coefficients.

Although this phenomenon is often blamed on forecasting inaccuracies or operational breakdowns, we argue it stems from risk-averse scheduling strategies. By applying a stochastic self-scheduling model to real-world data from the Australian National Electricity Market, we show that risk-averse storage units adopt a short-sighted operational approach. Specifically, they focus narrowly on immediate price arbitrage, targeting only prices exceeding a high threshold, which results in missed opportunities during moderate price spikes. These findings carry significant policy weight, particularly given the lack of transparency surrounding unit-level risk aversion and the potential necessity for regulators to make risk tolerance levels explicit. Ultimately, our results underscore the necessity of future scarcity management policies on storage based on robust, generalized forecasting tools.

The simplified model incorporates representative features of the real-world atmosphere, including land-sea distribution, topography, and orbital geometry. Land-sea configurations were selected to ensure the presence of western boundary currents, which are essential for generating a hot outer equator and conditions suitable for land formation. After verifying the model's capability to simulate the HIRAM's land-and-sea circulation, a suite of land scenarios was simulated to identify conditions conducive to land formation. Based on simulated palaeoclimate data, land formation conditions were categorized into three groups: (I) unlikely, (II) uncertain, and (III) probable. Specifically, when land was placed directly adjacent to the hot outer equator, the intense heat caused the land to subside beneath the sea level (category I). Conversely, lands positioned 0–5° latitude from the cool, dry, subtropical outer equator (up to 10° in certain cases) experienced significant soil formation (categories II and III). Furthermore, the width of the hot, humid, subtropical inner equator was found to be approximately 10° under current solar constant levels, though this could vary between 5° and 15° depending on the solar constant's magnitude. These findings are valuable for constraining land formation conditions in exoplanet research and palaeogeological analyses, and they indicate that the land found on current Earth was likely formed in position group (II) during the Mesoproterozoic or Neoproterozoic eras. Additionally, this study demonstrates that our method can estimate land formation conditions for atmospheres with different land-sea distributions, varying numbers and placements of continents, and diverse planetary parameters. The resulting land formation conditions can serve as a more realistic benchmark than existing criteria, such as the "warm and wet" condition, for assessing the habitability of exoplanets.

AL is particularly valuable in large-scale industrial applications where labeling expenses are high, prompting practitioners to utilize every available technique to enhance model accuracy. Consequently, validating the outcomes of AL methods against a representative holdout test set is standard practice. However, in many scenarios, securing even a small number of labels from the holdout set through human annotation is infeasible. To overcome this constraint, this paper introduces SemiSupervised Active Learning (SSL), an algorithm that leverages a fully unlabeled holdout set to boost the accuracy of DNNs trained on actively learned data. We demonstrate through experiments that SSL yields substantial improvements over traditional AL and can be integrated with any holdout dataset. Our experimental results on three image classification tasks show that both supervised and semi-supervised active learning strategies can achieve a 5% increase in model accuracy using only 10% additional labels. These findings indicate that SSL can significantly exceed the performance gains of conventional active learning approaches. To further validate our approach, we conducted a gradual label addition experiment on a natural image classification task, illustrating how the algorithm adapts across varying label counts. The code for our experiments is publicly available. SSL represents a straightforward and potent algorithm capable of extracting maximum value from active learning projects by utilizing all unlabeled data, free from common semi-supervised learning pitfalls such as overfitting on clean, noise-free unlabeled data and the need for substantial volumes of labels. Our results confirm that SSL can achieve a more than 50% accuracy boost with as few as 2,500 labels and a 25% boost with as few as 1,000 labels on our test sets. We employ ResNet-50 architectures trained on ImageNet for all our experiments.

Title: Enhancing Word Sense Disambiguation via Data Augmentation

Abstract: Although integrating lexical knowledge bases has shown promising results for word sense disambiguation (WSD), current methods often rely on hand-crafted context-gloss pairs, which can be scarce and costly to create. In this paper, we demonstrate that performance can be significantly improved through data augmentation. By evaluating multiple augmentation strategies on English WSD tasks, our experiments indicate that both gloss and context back-translation are effective. Furthermore, using hypernyms instead of hyponyms leads to performance gains. Our experiments with English WordNet and the multilingual OPUS parallel corpus show that these findings hold true even without leveraging high-resource languages. We also compared and analyzed the effectiveness of various hypernym extraction methods. Additionally, we examined the impact of noise introduced into translated contexts and glosses. We made both the raw data and our code public to facilitate future research into sense definitions and WSD. Experiments with the English MultiSenseEval dataset demonstrate that our enhanced model outperforms existing context-gloss based WSD systems. Moreover, experiments on the GLUE natural language understanding benchmark indicate that our model generalizes well to new tasks. We

Experiments conducted on the Spider dataset demonstrate that our framework outperforms baseline methods in both execution accuracy and exact set match accuracy, particularly when database contents are missing, with detailed analysis offering insights for future research. The proposed framework is open-source and accessible at https://github.com/MUGroup/DFSQL.

### Related Work

**Schema Linking**
Existing T2SQL research predominantly assumes a complete and accurate schema, a condition rarely met in real-world scenarios. Antol et al. highlighted the challenge of incomplete and incorrect database schemas in practical natural language understanding systems. Recent studies have attempted to mitigate this by integrating multi-source information or leveraging large language models (LLMs) for completion. In contrast, our work focuses on the more difficult and practical problem of incomplete schemas. Since synthesized SQL often contains incorrect table and column names due to missed table joins, we frame this as a distinct subtask of zero-shot semantic parsing: auxiliary column selection. Unlike multi-source information integration, this approach avoids the noise inherent in LLM-generated data. Our method leverages natural language descriptions to learn a representation of table similarity, enabling the model to identify the most relevant table for a given SELECT clause. This reinforces the encoder's capability to handle incomplete schemas and reduces the probability of erroneous table joins. Although we currently address the missing table head (SELECT clause), the proposed method is also applicable to other missing component scenarios. Furthermore, while prior works on incomplete schemas target T2SQL, our approach is applicable to any pipeline-based text-to-structure parsing task.

**Value Filling**
Current T2SQL pipelines typically comprise three stages: semantic parsing, code execution, and result verification. While prior efforts on incorrect schema handling focus on restoration (e.g., table and column name correction), our work addresses the issue of missing database contents. Existing parsers often substitute unavailable values with null or dummy data (e.g., 0), which can lead to incorrect results and failed execution verification. We explore two distinct approaches to address this problem. The first method assigns a default value based on the column's data type, whereas the second leverages context from similar questions within the same schema to infer missing values using a retriever

However, because CV relies on random data partitioning, the resulting performance estimates are stochastic and can exhibit significant variability, particularly in natural language processing (NLP). We show that such unstable estimates are unsuitable for effective parameter tuning; consequently, the selected parameters are highly sensitive to data splits, often leading to sub-optimal choices and severe reproducibility challenges.

To address this, we propose employing J-K-fold CV, which utilizes J independent K-fold cross-validations to assess performance. Our primary contributions involve extending J-K-fold CV to the domain of parameter tuning and exploring strategies for selecting optimal values for J and K. We argue that minimizing variability is more critical than reducing bias for successful tuning, advocating for lower-than-typical values of K in NLP literature. This allows computational resources to be redirected toward increasing J. To validate the broad applicability of our recommendations, we examine a diverse set of case studies, including sentiment classification (both general and target-specific), part-of-speech tagging, and document classification. Our findings offer guidance on choosing J and K for various scenarios and demonstrate that achieving stable performance estimates requires ten times more data than previously thought necessary. Collectively, these results underscore the importance of viewing random seeds as a model hyperparameter and establish that J-K-fold CV is an essential tool for obtaining unbiased performance estimates.

This study examines how public sector officials evaluate their reliance on Google, their awareness of algorithmic biases affecting search outcomes, and their experiences with algorithmic fatigue. Through a structured, in-depth interview process involving 30 information professionals—librarians, HR specialists, social workers, and government officials—we gathered extensive qualitative data. This work contributes to the emerging field of algorithmic fatigue by providing empirical evidence of its existence and offering practical strategies for management. **Methods:**  
1. Architecture and hyperparameter adjustments are conducted using a genetic algorithm that optimizes a population of MLPs, guided by the generalized Pareto front (GPF) and a cost function representing network complexity.  
2. An initial hyperparameter subset is identified and tested across 40 time series. For each series, the results are modeled with a Gaussian distribution and converted into random process characteristics, which serve as input for the genetic algorithm to determine the optimal architecture.  
3. A secondary architecture is then constructed and fine-tuned utilizing the process parameters from step 4 of step 2.  
4. The performance of these modified approaches is measured and contrasted against standard genetic algorithm optimization and several heuristic methods.

**Results:** The findings indicate that this two-step procedure yields superior outcomes compared to using a genetic algorithm alone. Specifically, the proposed approach achieves a 10% improvement in mean performance and a 15% enhancement in the count of top-performing results (defined as exceeding 90+ of the baseline performance threshold of 84) when evaluated on the M3 and COMMA dataset.

**Conclusion:** It is demonstrated that combining a GPF-based genetic algorithm with a specific tuning process enables the customization of MLP architecture and hyperparameters for individual time series. This results in a process that is both more efficient and effective than traditional optimization techniques.

Since the 1970s, a significant body of panel data research has examined the shift from cartel-dominated to price-taking industries using a specific random effects specification. However, this approach relies on two critical assumptions: route-specific effects remaining constant over time and measurement error being confined to the dependent variables. The new panel data on freight rates and volumes explicitly challenges both assumptions. Furthermore, secondary independent variables on technology and regulation, introduced after the cartel dissolution, indicate that at least one independent effect is not time-invariant post-1980. Violating the assumption of time-invariant route-specific effects leads to inconsistent standard errors and biased random effects estimates when such effects are present. Given these complexities, we advocate for a regression model with only time and route intercepts, random errors, and fixed effects for independent variables introduced after the cartel's end. This specification ensures that only the random error contains random components. Although this approach was critiqued by Hsiao (2005) for potential inefficiency with our specific panel dimensions, it guarantees consistency in fixed effects estimates and standard errors. We provide updated empirical results supporting this methodology.

By matching the scattering amplitudes between the two EFTs for this subprocess, we establish the correspondence between the leading coefficients in HEFT and SMEFT. Finally, we assess the sensitivity to these two dominant HEFT coefficients at CLIC (3 TeV, 5 ab$^{-1}$) and ILC (1 TeV, 8 ab$^{-1}$). We conclude by delineating the accessible parameter space for these coefficients, based on the scattered hadrons' kinematics, across both future linear colliders for the WW fusion process. Finally, we extend our analysis to include non-$WW$ fusion subprocesses. Standard model predictions and references are listed in the accompanying appendix. This work accompanies our previous publication [arXiv:2007.00305], where we examined the SMEFT for this same production channel.

This process begins with a specific parametrization of the geometry, termed 'pre-non-relativistic' parametrization, which reformulates general relativity to facilitate an analytical $1/c^2$ expansion. Furthermore, by leveraging the parametrization used to expand the action, we derive the Hamiltonian and Hamiltonian constraint in the same expansion, thereby establishing a complete Hamiltonian formulation of general relativity in the weak-field and slow-motion limits. To our knowledge, this represents the first derivation of the next-to-next-to-next-to-leading order in the Hamiltonian constraint. The results obtained in both the weak-field and full Hamiltonian constraints align with established findings in the literature. The systematic methodology employed in this study can be extended to derive the Hamiltonian and Hamiltonian constraint to higher orders in the $1/c^2$ expansion for any metric. However, such a generalization presents significant challenges, as the expressions for the Hamiltonian and constraint become increasingly intricate with higher-order expansions, ultimately rendering the procedure non-algorithmic. Consequently, this work establishes a comprehensive and systematic derivation of the Hamiltonian and Hamiltonian constraint in the weak-field and slow-motion limits, advancing beyond previous studies by field redefinitions that obscured the Newtonian limit. We anticipate that the techniques developed herein will prove beneficial in computing higher-order Post-Newtonian expansion coefficients. Specifically, our approach enables the derivation of the (3.5)th order in the Post-Newtonian expansion, currently the highest achieved order for the single-body problem and the third order for the binary-body problem. Moreover, our results may find applications in analyzing self-gravitating systems, such as stars and black holes, within the weak-field and slow-motion regimes.

Using polystyrene and hydrogel grains with diameter $d$, we examine materials exhibiting high and negligible contact friction, respectively. Drag forces were measured for orientations both perpendicular ($F_\perp$) and parallel ($F_\parallel$) to the cylinder's axis across a range of speeds $U$, spanning from quasi-static to rate-dependent regimes. Results indicate that the drag anisotropy ratio, $\xi = F_\perp/F_\parallel$, is not constant but rises substantially with both the driving rate and the aspect ratio $L/D$ in both granular media. Specifically, for $L/D = 20$, $\xi$ increases from 2.6 to 4.5 in high-friction beds and from 7.0 to 8.6 in low-friction beds as the nondimensional Froude number $Fr = U/\sqrt{g(D+d)}$ varies between $10^{-4}$ and $2 \times 10^{-2}$. Additionally, $L/D = 4$ cylinders composed of 500 segments were employed to trace stress field developments. We observe that $\xi$ grows logarithmically with $L/D$ for small aspect ratios in high-friction beds, adhering to the scaling $\xi = a + b\ln(L/D)$. In contrast, $\xi$ remains nearly constant in low-friction beds, suggesting an intrinsic length scale emerges from the interplay of $D$ and $d$. Furthermore, the drag coefficient $f = F/DL$ exhibits weak power-law dependence on $U$, where the exponent $n$ in $f \propto U^n$ depends on contact friction: $n \approx 0.3$ for high-friction beds and $n \approx 0.15$ for low-friction beds. Stress visualization in hydrogel beds reveals an hourglass-shaped pattern during transverse motion and two distinct stress cones aligned with the cylinder's axis during parallel motion. Finally, we discuss how these stress field observations account for the emergence of $\xi$ in both materials. Collectively, our data offer profound insights into the physics governing the orientation and traversal of wires and cylinders through granular environments.

There is a well-established history of analyzing and creating structure-preserving discretization methods, ranging from proving that standard schemes retain these properties to designing novel high-order schemes that exactly preserve them. However, when combined with implicit time-stepping, a significant drawback is that these properties typically depend on solving the potentially nonlinear systems of equations exactly at each time step. While feasible for small systems within floating-point precision, this approach becomes impractical for the large linear systems encountered in typical space-time PDE discretizations. This paper introduces a modification to the standard flexible generalized minimum residual (FGMRES) iteration that imposes selected constraints on approximate numerical solutions. We illustrate its effectiveness by applying it to both conservation law systems and dissipative systems. Specifically, for systems of PDES defining strongly coupled nonlinear diffusive processes, we demonstrate that our proposed constraint strategy enables the numerical solution of large systems (around $10^6$ dimensions) to exactly satisfy key geometric structures of the underlying physical models. These systems arise from applying a high-order spatial discontinuous Galerkin method to a system of nonlinear diffusion equations featuring a degenerate diffusivity proportional to a power law of the unknown. Implicit time-stepping transforms this system into a nonlinear variational problem where the exact solution must conserve the entropy of the system. Although the exact solution is unattainable due to spatial discretization in certain regimes, we show that the time-stepped system can be solved to high accuracy, preserving the entropy at every time step. To achieve this, we employ a monolithic solution strategy that jointly discretizes space and time. Specifically, we derive a second-order in time, high-order in space strong time marching scheme and a fully implicit Runge-Kutta scheme based on the gear method for spatial discretization. This scheme utilizes convex optimization to determine numerical fluxes, ensuring third-order accuracy in space at interfaces between discontinuous Galerkin polynomial coefficients where the flux is minimum/maximum. Regarding time accuracy, we achieve third-order accuracy up to third-order terms of $\Delta t$. These results extend to a generalized system of nonlinear diffusion equations.

Originating in the 1970s through the work of Las Vergnas and Häggkvist, the investigation of graphs with the PMH-property integrates three fundamental graph concepts: matchings, Hamiltonicity, and edge-colourings. Throughout the paper, we illustrate our constructions and occupy constructions with numerous figures. The results are further visualized via an interactive application that also serves to explain the concepts of Petrie duals and PMH-matchings. All code used to generate our family of non-PMH cubic graphs and their associated PMH-matchings is available on GitHub.

where even intelligent or negligent decisions in pivotal moments can alter the match outcome. Consequently, players, coaches, and scouts seek to identify the optimal actions during critical phases, such as high-risk scenarios involving potential loss of possession or scoring opportunities. This study introduces a novel state representation for soccer combined with sequential modeling techniques to calculate the "tension" of any given game state—a metric reflecting the outcome's dependence on future actions. Our model, which processes statistical data relevant to potential losses or goals, operates without supervision regarding actual match results. Despite using relatively modest input data, the proposed framework outperforms baseline models in prediction tasks. Specifically, when trained solely on data from the 20 minutes preceding halftime or the final 20 minutes, the model learned to forecast three distinct "tension" values corresponding to the probable outcomes (goal, no goal, or game over). Furthermore, evidence suggests the model also internalized a fourth state representing the "scored goal" scenario. By visualizing the model's internal representations, we confirmed its ability to distinguish between these four states. Additionally, we demonstrated that data from specific matches contains sufficient information for the model to learn representations capable of predicting "tension" values across any game state. Finally, we highlighted how our approach offers insights into soccer dynamics that conventional statistical analyses often overlook. Since the model identifies states that are information-rich regarding the outcome, it can pinpoint critical game moments, thereby offering a straightforward and quantitative method for identifying "critical moments" in soccer. The code is accessible at https://github.com/mohsensharifi/tension.

Question: Can the proposed model forecast three distinct "tension" values based on soccer game data? Answer: Yes.

Question: What does the model's internal representation evidence suggest, in addition to the three "tension" values? Answer: A fourth state representing "scored goal".

Question: What is the main objective of using the proposed state representation and sequential modeling methods in soccer? Answer: To calculate "tension" in any game state, a metric that quantizes the outcome's dependence on future actions.

immigration and a competition-dispersal tradeoff jointly influence the dynamics of two species competing for space on regular lattices. In this system, one species can invade only nearest-neighbor sites, whereas the other species can invade sites at any distance but possesses lower local competitiveness, establishing with a probability $g \le 1$. Immigration is incorporated as external noise that spontaneously replaces an individual at a lattice site with one from the opposing species. This interplay of mechanisms generates diverse competitive outcomes, ranging from the exclusion of one species to mono-stable coexistence at fixed population ratios, as well as bi-stable coexistence where population proportions depend on initial conditions. Notably, within the bi-stable regime, increasing immigration intensity beyond a critical threshold triggers a discontinuous transition. This results in a "half loop" dynamics characteristic of a cusp catastrophe, ultimately causing the irreversible extinction of the species with the limited dispersal range. This extinction threshold is lower than the cutoff in the absence of asymmetry, highlighting the role of competition against spontaneous immigration in driving extinctions. The model extends to scenarios with stochastic internal exchanges (species attempting to occupy neighboring sites of the other species) and, with parameter adjustments, recapitulates the main findings. Additionally, the framework can be adapted to represent the competition between natural and invasive species. These results align with previous theoretical and experimental observations regarding the impact of noise on competition-dispersal tradeoffs [T. Rieder and G. Sz\"agyner, J. Stat. Phys. 174, 1080 (2019); P. Lechat and M. Droesbeke, Phys. Rev. E 100, 022404 (2019)] and are explained by a mean-field theory. This theory accounts for the coexistence phases and the non-trustable half loop dynamics by analyzing the Jacobian matrix of the mean-field equations at the extinction points of the two populations, which occurs when the net growth rate of the species with limited dispersal reaches zero. We also investigate the universality of this half loop dynamics and find that, while the mean-field description yields a standard cusp catastrophe, the half loop emerges because the parameter controlling the dispersion competition is fixed. Furthermore, the mean-field approach reveals a linear increase in the extinction threshold with the internal exchange probability, a result verified numerically. However, when this internal exchange probability is zero, the half loop arises from the non-zero minimum of the mean-field description.

By incorporating uncertainties related to luminosity measurements and relativistic beaming, we examine the implications for these properties in X-ray selected Active Galactic Nuclei that exhibit varying levels of optical emission lines. In these contexts, physically viable code patterns are inherently non-negative, systematically structured, and often lack the incoherence properties found in other patterns like Gaussian codes, which can hinder reconstruction quality. This paper addresses this by designing code patterns for video compressed sensing and demosaicing that minimize the mutual coherence of the matrix $\boldsymbol{\Phi\Psi}$, where $\boldsymbol{\Phi}$ is the sensing matrix derived from the code and $\boldsymbol{\Psi}$ represents the signal basis. Our primary contribution lies in explicitly incorporating the specific structural constraints required by these applications: (1) non-negativity, (2) block-diagonal structure, and (3) circular shifting. Notably, the circular shifting property facilitates accurate and seamless patch-wise reconstruction within certain compressed sensing frameworks. To achieve this, we employ an adaptive genetic algorithm (AGA) to optimize the sub-block-diagonal components of the block-diagonal matrix. Validation across both synthetic and real-world data confirms that these new codes yield superior reconstruction results; specifically, the mean squared error (MSE) of reconstructed frames in compressed sensing videos and the individual patch reconstructions in demosaicing exceeds that of methods using random random Gaussian (RRG) patterns and other existing codes by more than an order of magnitude. Furthermore, compared to recent state-of-the-art methods (Ref. ~\cite{Sohrab22a}, Sobarb22b), the proposed approach requires roughly 50\% fewer training samples for equivalent performance. Yarkovsky-O'Keefe-Radzievskii-Paddack (YORP) effect, a net torque generated by the reflection and thermal re-emission of solar radiation from their surfaces. This phenomenon causes a gradual alteration in rotation periods, which is most readily observable in light curves due to the quadratic accumulation of phase shifts over time. We gathered archived light curves and conducted new photometric observations for asteroids (10115) 1992 SK, (1620) Geographos, and (1685) Toro. Using light curve inversion, we fitted the data to convex shape models, modeling the YORP effect as a linear variation in rotation frequency ($\upsilon \equiv \mathrm{d}\omega / \mathrm{d}t$) and optimizing it alongside other spin and shape parameters. For asteroid (10115) 1992 SK, we detected a rotational acceleration of $\upsilon = (8.3 \pm 0.6) \times 10^{-8}\,\mathrm{rad}\,\mathrm{d}^{-2}$, which aligns well with YORP calculations based on our own shape model. For (1685) Toro, we measured $\upsilon = (3.3 \pm 0.3) \times 10^{-7}\,\mathrm{rad}\,\mathrm{d}^{-2}}$, representing the most significant YORP acceleration recorded to date for this asteroid. Conversely, our results indicate that asteroid (1620) Geographos likely experiences a deceleration, though this is at odds with YORP predictions. We note that while a mass-distribution anomaly could theoretically produce such deceleration, no corresponding surface features have been identified. Consequently, we speculate that unmodeled non-gravitational forces, such as outgassing, might be the underlying cause.

When restricted to the one-way model, these transducers characterize rational functions. Despite the robust characterization of regular functions by various finite-state devices, even the subclass of rational functions may include functions that are not computable by a Turing machine with infinite input. This paper introduces a decision procedure for the synthesis problem: given a regular function $f$ (specified by one of the aforementioned transducer models), determine if $f$ is computable, and if so, construct a Turing machine that computes it. For regular functions, we demonstrate that computability is equivalent to continuity, thereby reducing the problem to deciding continuity. We provide a generic characterization of continuity for functions that preserve regular languages under inverse image, such as regular functions, and utilize this to prove the decidability of continuity (and consequently computability) for both rational and regular functions. For rational functions, we show that this decision can be made in $\mathsf{NLogSpace}$ (previously established as $\mathsf{PTime}$ by Prieur). Similarly, we effectively characterize the uniform continuity of regular functions and connect it to the concept of uniform computability, which provides stronger efficiency assurances. While uniform computability for infinite input is generally undecidable, we prove that it is decidable for regular functions. This extends previous work on the topic [C.S. Calude et al., 2009]. Additionally, we examine the complexity of determining whether a function is uniformly continuous or uniformly computable on restricted domains, such as within a specific language or on "most" infinite words. Our findings generalize to finite-state transducers producing outputs in any effective topological space. To support these results, we develop novel techniques for characterizing uniformly continuous and uniformly computable functions on regular languages, particularly for data words with infinite domains.

A simplified variant, called next-generation reservoir computing (NGRC), further streamlines the process by eliminating many algorithmic hyperparameters to automatically identify high-performing traditional reservoir computers. This study examines a difficult scenario involving a dynamical system with multiple co-existing attractors and disparate time scales. These findings reinforce the superior learning capabilities of this new algorithm for modeling dynamical systems. The system studied serves as a benchmark in nonlinear science for its ability to produce multiple stable states from simple equations, including oscillations, chaos, and stationary states. The source data is openly available, enabling easy testing on other systems. Notably, NGRC's significant reduction in hyperparameters makes it especially useful in applications where training data is limited, such as neuroscience and meteorology. The approach also effectively handles real-world data, as demonstrated by our accurate prediction of the sleep cycle from actual human EEG recordings.
