While the visual categorization hypothesis attributes this continuum to the presence of animal-specific features, the agency hypothesis suggests it reflects the representation of agents. In this study, we tested both theories using an fMRI adaptation task where 20 participants viewed images organized into four quadrants, each containing four categories. Categories in the top two quadrals shared the same animacy level (high or low) and were manipulated based on the animal features theory, whereas those in the bottom two quadrals shared animacy level and were manipulated according to the agency theory. fMRI adaptation results indicated that animacy is encoded as a continuum in VTC. Both types of manipulations produced identical patterns of animacy organization, as both involve the capacity to initiate action. These findings reject the visual categorization hypothesis and support the broader category of agency as the organizing principle for animacy. Furthermore, this result aligns with the functional specialization of VTC for object agency. To our knowledge, this is the first study to demonstrate that animal features do not structure the animacy continuum in VTC. Our findings suggest that this continuum is better explained by the capacity to initiate action and may even be downstream from visual categorization within this region. These conclusions are consistent with a gradual transition from posterior to anterior VTC, reflecting increasing complexity in visual object representations. (Abstract provided by the author)

While prior research has established the existence of this issue, our work conducts novel investigations to quantify the bias, identify its root causes, and propose mitigation strategies. First, we establish analytical inequalities that bound the mean-square bias across all possible physical maps to examine the problem in an abstract framework. Neural network quantum states (NQS) have emerged as a flexible framework for simulating quantum many-body systems. These models demonstrate that even with a minimal variational distance from the target wavefunction, key physical observables can scale efficiently with system size. However, the gradient-based optimization routines typically used to train NQS often struggle with large system sizes due to the high computational cost of calculating the action. To overcome this, we introduce a Monte Carlo technique based on the Hasell-Hutchinson estimator. This method estimates the gradient of the log norm with cubic scaling relative to the lattice size $N$. Our results indicate a quadratic speedup in wall-clock time when training NQS to the same fidelity compared to traditional methods.

The Variational Quantum Neural Network (VQNN) architecture, which employs stochastic gradient descent to optimize parameters, has achieved state-of-the-art results in simulating lattice gauge theories. This paper seeks to enhance the cross-task generalization capabilities of large-scale multi-task language models, such as T0 and FLAN, within an unsupervised framework. We introduce ReCross, a retrieval-augmentation approach that utilizes a few unlabeled examples as queries to fetch a targeted subset of upstream data, thereby updating the model to improve its generalization performance. ReCross represents a simple yet potent retrieval strategy that integrates efficient dense retrieval with effective pairwise reranking. Empirical results and analysis demonstrate that our method significantly surpasses both non-retrieval approaches and other baseline techniques. Furthermore, we offer insights into how this process activates distinct neural pathways in the model compared to standard multi-task learning methods. By combining the T0 foundation with our proposed retrieval scheme, we have developed an unsupervised task adapter that outperforms state-of-the-art automated evaluations. This adapter achieves state-of-the-art results on 25 datasets across diverse domains, including natural inference, common sense reasoning, reading comprehension, language understanding, and code evaluation. Our foundation (crossT0), available alongside the adapter for other unlabeled datasets, exceeds the performance of T0, ALPAGAFew, and few-shot PaLM across numerous downstream evaluations. CrossT0 exhibits superior generalization in a variety of few-shot scenarios and demonstrates a heightened sensitivity to data contamination. Furthermore, we observe that even simple retrieval mechanisms can yield significant improvements over baselines in unsupervised data selection. The proposed retrieval approach is concise, computationally efficient, and highly effective.

Automatic data selection for domain adaptation has gained significant attention in recent years. However, most existing approaches rely on supervised techniques that require a small number of labeled target samples for tuning. In this study, we address the core limitation of current methods by proposing a framework that integrates the strengths of unsupervised and few-shot data selection. Extensive cross-validations demonstrate that our model effectively removes systematics, yielding significant improvements over previous methods. Specifically, the negative luminosity dependence observed in [Mg/H] versus log(g) in DR16 data has been successfully eliminated in DR17. Furthermore, the residual plots for DR17 exhibit narrower distributions with reduced widths, indicating minimal non-linear trends or luminosity-dependent systematic errors. We estimate the DR17 systematic uncertainties at approximately 0.01–0.02 dex for most elements, with the exception of Li, Na, and Ni, which range from 0.04 to 0.06 dex. These DR17 uncertainties are roughly half the size of those for DR16 and DR15. Our DR17 results align well with published DR15 measurements from high-quality spectrographs for well-studied elements and stars. By leveraging the vast number of APOGEE spectra, we derived novel trends for metallicities in the solar neighborhood that were previously inaccessible. These findings serve as both diagnostics and priors to identify and mitigate DR17 systematics in luminosity-dependent ways for bright, metal-poor, and giant stars in future data releases. Specifically, we identified a magnitude-dependent systematic error for [Ni/H] in DR17 for giants between $F_{JPS} \sim 14$ and 16 mag (~0.04 dex) and a magnitude-independent error of $\sim -0.03$ dex for stars with $F_{JPS} < 14$ mag, the latter likely arising from contamination by He I lines. These results demonstrate that DR17 exhibits the smallest luminosity-dependent systematic uncertainties for metallicities, marking the first detection of Ni and most other light elements (excluding Li and Na) in the local galactic disk.

-19 pandemic rapidly spread globally, causing severe repercussions in China. During this period, online rumors and fear regarding the virus intensified, peaking in the first half of February 2020 before declining in later months. Existing rumor datasets are often limited, making it challenging to construct a comprehensive historical dataset that captures both the magnitude and trajectory of rumors. This study utilizes a metric rooted in social media information theory—redundancy, which reflects the degree of similarity among pieces of information—to extract rumors from WeChat public accounts. By applying this method to trillions of articles, we assembled a complete dataset of viral information, offering new insights into the magnitude and timeline of rumors. validated against manual classification, our analysis revealed that the predominant rumors were false, originating from non-human sources and targeting specific vulnerable groups. These findings underscore the necessity of timely, accurate, and accessible information dissemination. Furthermore, the account behaviors driving rumor spread shifted from fear-based to deception-based as the epidemic progressed. Ultimately, this paper presents a novel, multi-indicator framework for extracting rumors and demonstrates how integrating several indicators yields superior detection results, thereby establishing a robust methodology for future epidemic rumor extraction.

Since this phenomenon markedly affects both the thermal and mechanical characteristics of these materials, it must be accounted for in manufacturing planning and product applications. To simultaneously represent both effects, the proposed model employs a triple decomposition of the deformation gradient. Furthermore, it utilizes a thermodynamic framework grounded in the Coleman–Noll procedure and the principle of minimum dissipation potential, which necessitates specific assumptions regarding the Helmholtz free energy and the dissipation potential. This paper revisits the topic using a quantum thermodynamic framework, specifically calculating two key quantities: heat capacity and quantum compressibility for model geometries containing quantum fields at both high and low temperatures. Abstract: Recent advancements in text-to-attribution models have revealed a systematic bias toward internal factors (such as subject and emotion) when generating attributions for human text summaries, a trend that recent text generation models continue to exhibit. This study investigates the root causes of this bias by examining the learning process of a text-to-attribution model using atomic knowledge from the COMMA dataset. Our findings indicate that while atomic knowledge itself is not inherently biased, its organization favors internal factors, resulting in a "recency effect" where later-added attributes are more likely to be selected as key factors. To demonstrate the practical significance of this insight, we redesigned the atomic knowledge structure and showed that this change eliminates the bias against external factors (such as topic and report) in model-generated attributions. These results suggest a potential solution to mitigate existing biases in text-to-attribution models.

Although the mean-variance optimization problem can be formulated as a system of linear equations using Lagrange multipliers—potentially enabling the exponential speedup of the HHL quantum algorithm—many components of HHL are incompatible with current Noisy Intermediate Scale Quantum (NISQ) hardware. This paper presents NISQ-HHL, the first hybrid adaptation of HHL designed for end-to-end execution of small-scale portfolio optimization on NISQ devices. NISQ-HHL builds upon existing hybrid HHL variants by leveraging new hardware capabilities, including mid-circuit measurement, qubit reset and reuse, and Quantum Conditional Logic (QCL). To our knowledge, this is the first algorithm to implement a QCL-enhanced Phase Estimation on real trapped-ion hardware, specifically the Quantinuum System Model H1-1. Furthermore, the work introduces a novel technique for determining the optimal evolution time for Hamiltonian simulation. Although the primary focus is on portfolio optimization, the proposed methods for scaling HHL are broadly applicable to any problem solvable via HHL within the NISQ era. Although the empirical analysis centers on portfolio optimization and the specific characteristics of the Quantinuum H1-1 processor, the paper provides comprehensive guidelines for implementing the algorithm on other NISQ processors. Ultimately, this research underscores the potential of qubit reset and quantum conditional operations as powerful tools for operating Hamiltonian-based algorithms on near-term quantum computers. Video view prediction involves generating video content from a new camera viewpoint using clips from one or more existing perspectives. While recent studies address this challenge, they often struggle with substantial viewpoint changes, exhibit failures in complex scenes, and require training on a target view that is uncommon in practical applications. By leveraging both view-dependent and global representations, the method overcomes obstacles associated with significant viewpoint shifts, including occlusions and reflections, by integrating complementary information from source views to predict target content. In this study, we experimentally demonstrate using femtosecond laser writing that fundamental and excited orbital states can couple when situated at distinct spatial locations. We provide a comprehensive characterization of an asymmetric double-well-like potential and employ a scanning method to effectively map dynamics along the propagation axis. Leveraging the phase structure of higher-order photonic modes and the effective negative coupling generated, we propose a trimer configuration functioning as a phase beam splitter ($\pi$-BS), offering significant potential for multiplexing and interference-based photonic concatenated operations. Our experimental findings align remarkably well with theoretical models built upon the Bloch Hamiltonian and effective coupling parameters, thereby establishing a new framework for designing and understanding photonic metamaterials and multiplexing mechanisms via orbital states. Consequently, the experimentally established effective coupling, which behaves as if the orbitals were closer together, can drive various self-consistent phenomena such as effective tunneling, long-range hopping, exchange interaction, virtual coupling generation, and multiple bond formations (single, double, and triple bonds). This phenomenon has been observed in various systems, including graphene and ferromagnetic layers. Manipulating spin-orbit coupling offers a potential route to uncover novel and exotic phases within superconducting and semimetallic systems. In this study, we investigate the magnetoelectrical transport properties—specifically magnetoresistance and the anomalous Hall effect—in Cobalt/Bismuth multilayers to identify signatures of the spin-orbit proximity effect and determine its origin. Our findings suggest an increase in the spontaneous magnetic moment of Bismuth layers induced by the Cobalt layers. Furthermore, analysis of the anomalous Hall effect indicates a modification in the Bismuth's semimetal character attributable to the spin-orbit proximity effect: the Fermi surface nesting responsible for the effect becomes more pronounced, and the mobility of hole-like carriers rises significantly. Additionally, we observe a reduction in electron-like carriers and a shift in the Hall effect contribution from the intrinsic to the extrinsic mechanism. These alterations in the Bismuth's band structure are interpreted as consequences of hybridization between Bismuth and Cobalt orbitals at their interface. Moreover, a model based on spin-orbit scattering at the Bismuth/Cobalt interface accounts for the observed spontaneous magnetization of Bismuth and the evolution of its anomalous Hall effect. This model implies that increasing spin-orbit scattering at the interface can induce a nesting of the Fermi surface, resulting in an "imperfect" Weyl semi-metal state in Bismuth. The impact of these effects on the superconductivity of such a state represents a topic for future research. (DOI: 10.1103/PhysRevB.97.115423)

Furthermore, we develop and introduce simple, reliable, and interpretable visualizations of the uncertainty estimates. These uncertainties are highest in regions with low probability—potentially indicating hallucinations—and align with voxel-level heteroscedasticity in the reference images. Additionally, we show that incorporating real-world, low-count OOD PET data enhances the model's performance on in-distribution datasets. Ultimately, the findings from both quantitative analyses and visualizations support the necessity of accounting for OOD data distribution shifts when training DNNs for PET imaging applications.

This study explores the relationship between Centering Theory and contemporary coreference resolution systems. We propose an operational definition of centering and employ a search-based methodology to systematically evaluate whether neural coreference resolvers comply with CT rules through various discourse metrics. Our information-theoretic analysis indicates a positive correlation between coreference and centering, yet demonstrates that high-performing neural resolvers gain little advantage from explicitly modeling centering concepts. Furthermore, we find that contextualized embeddings encapsulate much of the necessary coherence information, explaining why neural systems achieve minimal improvement when provided with explicit centering features. Finally, we address several open queries regarding coreference and discourse modeling, including potential issues with current evaluation methods, contextualized embeddings, and the integration of centering features. Overall, this paper provides novel insights into coreference modeling from a centering theory perspective and contributes new findings on coreference evaluation and feature selection. We release our data and scripts to facilitate future research into coreference and centering. Our results suggest that while CT validates coreference as the primary driver of local discourse coherence, it is not strictly obligatory; furthermore, modern neural resolvers underutilize utterance-level contextual information regarding coreference, although they implicitly absorb sentence-level context. To leverage CT fully, utterance-level representations must be enhanced with entity-based world knowledge. While CT offers a straightforward model of local discourse coherence, extending it to a broader scope could yield significant benefits for coreference resolution.

WiFi fingerprinting, which involves gathering Received Signal Strength Indicator (RSSI) measurements at known locations, is a prevalent technique in various positioning algorithms found in existing literature. However, accurately calculating the spatial distance between fingerprints is highly dependent on the choice of signal distance function used to map signal space to geospatial distance. This study proposes leveraging machine learning to enhance the estimation of geospatial distances between fingerprints. To develop a generalizable model applicable to any indoor setting, the research analyzed data from 13 diverse open datasets. The novel approach identified key features by evaluating common signal distance metrics through a feature selection process that combined feature analysis with a genetic algorithm. To ensure venue independence, all models were evaluated on datasets that were not used during training or validation. Finally, multiple machine learning algorithms were compared using a comprehensive range of evaluation metrics, including their capacity to scale from controlled test beds to real-world, unsolicited datasets. The findings demonstrate that estimating geospatial distances between RSSI fingerprints can be accomplished accurately and without bias toward a specific location, achieving a mean error of 2.33 meters across seven datasets. Furthermore, the study reveals that the effectiveness of certain feature selection methods and machine learning algorithms varies by venue, emphasizing the potential benefit of deploying localized models. The source code for all models and their evaluation on multiple datasets is publicly available.

We attempted to synthesize a one-year set of ASM images by applying ML techniques to a "blind" dataset derived from short-exposure (64 s) source maps (SEMs). Each agent selects an action to maximize her own value, conditioned on the choices made by preceding agents. Our objective is to identify action sequences that achieve a total social welfare close to the optimal solution. We assume the ability to query the value $v_i(S)$ obtained by agent $i$ when acting after the set of agents $S$. To minimize the welfare gap between the solution produced by an algorithm and the optimal solution, we aim to reduce the number of queries required. We establish query complexity lower bounds demonstrating that, even with simple valuations such as submodular or $X$-concave functions, $\Omega(n)$ and $\Omega(n^2)$ queries are necessarily required to achieve near-optimal solutions for $n$ agents. Furthermore, we introduce several algorithmic results with associated query complexity analyses. Notably, we present an generalization of value-based rounding—extending beyond submodular valuations to $X$-concave valuations—with its analysis of the necessary $O(n \log n)$ queries. Additionally, we examine the case where valuations are black-box stochastic, showing that an efficient algorithm exists achieving a $2$-approximation with high probability using $O(n^2 \log n)$ queries. Finally, we detail an algorithm for the offline setting where all valuations are known, which achieves an optimal $n$-approximation with exactly $n$ queries. In summary, our contributions include strong query complexity lower bounds for the $n$-agent case and various algorithms ranging from general frameworks to specialized settings, along with tight or near-tight query complexity analyses. This work underscores the feasibility of integrating mechanisms from operations research into fields like artificial intelligence and game theory.

These techniques were subsequently applied to Pan-STARRS1 images of main belt asteroids ranging from 4 to 60 km in diameter. Since Johnston (2019) reports fewer than 10 known binaries in this size category with separations exceeding 10% of the primary's Hill radius, finding additional wide binaries is essential for determining the limits of binary stability and refining our understanding of asteroid masses. Our analysis involved two steps: first, comparing the major axis orientation of an asteroid's elliptical PSF against its non-sidereal sky rate, and second, contrasting the one-dimensional median profile (generated by collapsing the image along the direction of motion) with that of nearby field stars. We flagged results that significantly deviated from expected single-asteroid measurements, and the targets with the highest number of flags were selected as binary candidates for confirmation using high-acuity imaging. This approach led to the discovery of four new wide-binary asteroids: two (2015 MZ5 and 2012 SF21) were later verified via adaptive optics imaging, one (2008 DV2) was confirmed through subsequent high-acuity observations, and the origin of the final candidate (2004 GU5) remains unconfirmed. These discoveries demonstrate that wide binaries are prevalent among mid-sized main belt asteroids, suggesting that approximately 30% of this population may constitute binary systems. While the typical wide-separation binary consists of a main-body asteroid and a satellite roughly one-fifth the size of the main body (specifically, 2015 MZ5 has a 1.9 km satellite and 2012 SF21 has a 3.0 km satellite), this configuration is significantly wider than the median binary in this population (about 6 arcseconds or 1.0 Hill radii), where satellites are typically smaller than 1 km. This size discrepancy implies that wide-separation binaries may have formed via different mechanisms than close-orbit binaries. Furthermore, this population likely includes systems interacting with triples and hierarchical triples, which are relevant to models of main belt evolution and the origin of near-Earth asteroids. The techniques described here can be easily adapted to data from other wide-field surveys, such as the main belt of planet-hunting missions like JWST and Roman.

To address these challenges, we introduce CodeT5-small, a compact transformer architecture designed for text-to-code and text completion tasks. We achieve competitive performance by fine-tuning this small model alongside a semantic pretraining strategy. Our contributions include a high-quality, multi-genere English code dataset (MPLEval) that encompasses 10 common program completion datasets, enabling efficient and effective training. Recent research categorizes the topology and geometry of knotted proteins by examining the distribution of their planar projections through topological entities known as knotoids. We adopt a similar analytical framework by developing a topologically grounded statistical metric to compare knotoid distributions among proteins sharing the same topology. Our method identifies geometric variations between trefoil proteins by quantifying their entanglement and successfully recovers clusters based on sequence similarity. By directly investigating the geometry and topology of native states, we can explore distinct folding pathways in proteins that form open-ended trefoil knots. Notably, our pipeline indicates that the folding process of shallowly knotted Carbonic Anhydrases involves the formation of a double-looped structure, a finding that contrasts with previous observations regarding deeply knotted trefoil proteins. We corroborate these results using Molecular Dynamics simulations. Furthermore, we estimate the proportion of proteins capable of adopting knotted configurations and identify the specific topological features of these proteins that facilitate or hinder their folding. Our comprehensive, quantitative approach offers a robust framework for evaluating the foldability of novel knotted proteins. The efficacy of our pipeline is demonstrated through various models, including simple polypeptide chains, knotted foldamers, and naturally occurring proteins. Our discoveries enhance current understanding of how proteins with distinct topologies and geometries influence their folding dynamics. A quasi-Heisenberg algebra is identified as a generic feature across various symmetry-breaking schemes of the anomalous NG theorem; this algebra suggests a violation or modification of the Heisenberg uncertainty relation within the NG sector, a phenomenon that is potentially verifiable experimentally. The formalism of the effective potential is introduced to elucidate the mechanism of the anomalous NG theorem using the derived Lie algebra results. Following an investigation into Lie algebra structures characteristic of Lorentz-symmetry-violated systems, a specific k-deformed Lie algebra is established to examine the counting law for NG bosons in this specific scenario. This approach offers a microscopic basis for a recently proposed phenomenological model in high-energy physics. The k-deformed algebra indicates that the conventional counting law is not the sole possibility; the difference between the would-be and physical NG bosons is determined by a discrete function involving modular arithmetic. This finding implies a novel violation or modification of the uncertainty relation, an effect that can be experimentally tested through precision measurements of the mass of the previously assumed NG boson. Furthermore, the quantum statistical properties of the k-deformed would-be and physical NG bosons are explored, a topic that has not been previously reported. Finally, the concept of dynamical restoration of Lorentz symmetry is discussed based on the findings from the k-deformed algebra. The ultimate goal is to provide a rigorous theoretical framework employing the exact Lie algebra of the Lorentz-symmetry-violated system to theoretically validate the phenomenological model regarding the CPT-odd Lorentz-symmetry violation coefficient recently observed in high-energy physics. This approach may facilitate theoretical progress in elucidating current enigmatic high-energy physics phenomena.

The planning of the selection phase comprises multiple challenges, each corresponding to established computing problems. While extensive research exists for these issues individually, studies adopting an integrated perspective are rare. This paper focuses on two critical components of application processing: the manual video screening phase and interview scheduling. Handoff criteria are dynamically determined by the system's handoff matrix and the specific requirements of every application. Additionally, the proposed DSS respects constraint satisfaction problems (CSPs) during interview scheduling, incorporating candidate preferences and interviewer availability. The defining characteristic of this process, which sets it apart from standard leptoquark pair production, is that the two leptoquarks generated in proton-proton collisions via $t$-channel lepton exchange are not charge conjugates; consequently, the term "asymmetric leptoquark pair production" is applied. We detail the necessary conditions for this mechanism to function and list all viable combinations of leptoquark multiplets capable of producing it. Furthermore, we conduct several phenomenological analyses within various simple scalar leptoquark extensions of the Standard Model to illustrate how to correctly incorporate asymmetric pair production into the reinterpretation of current experimental data, thereby yielding precise constraints on the parameter space. These computations are implemented in the public FIDO code. Our findings demonstrate that incorporating asymmetric pair production can lead to substantially tighter bounds on scalar leptoquark masses compared to scenarios considering only symmetric pairs ($s$-channel exchange), or even combine decays and single production cross sections. Specifically, for certain parameter combinations, the exclusion region can shift from approximately 800~GeV to over 1~TeV. This represents the most stringent limits ever recorded for any single type of scalar leptoquark and can exclude phenomenologically relevant areas of the parameter space that have previously evaded detection. These results are directly applicable to the interpretation of latest experimental searches, including those from the High-Luminosity LHC. As emphasized by recent studies, ignoring asymmetric pair production may result in underestimating the sensitivity of future colliders to scalar leptoquarks. Although this mechanism was first described for scalar leptoquarks, it is universally applicable to all spin states and thus affects searches for any type of leptoquark.

We begin by outlining the fundamental characteristics of the classic Kermack-McKendrick models before exploring their generalizations and applications to contact networks, viral co-circulation, epidemic curve trajectories, and incubation period distributions. Collectively, these models serve as foundational tools for quantifying the spread, severity, and duration of contact network epidemics and their associated outcomes. Contact network metrics, including basic and effective reproduction numbers, are identified as critical factors influencing the system's long-term behavior and potential stable states. Furthermore, we analyze models reflecting the impact of control measures on these network metrics and their direct consequences on health system capacity, hospitalization rates, and mortality. Finally, we consider models that account for population heterogeneity, such as variations in age, comorbidities, and adherence to control protocols. These discussions offer insights into how network contact changes—driven by interventions like school closures, non-essential business shutdowns, mask mandates, and vaccination—affect the "shape" of contact network curves and the system's stable states, thereby determining the trajectory of the contact network's evolution over time. Contact network models provide a robust framework for evaluating the potential impacts of control measures and vaccination strategies on the trajectory towards long-term stability. Consequently, understanding and monitoring the evolution of contact network metrics and their effects on critical health outcomes are essential for effectively managing contact network epidemics. This approach was successfully demonstrated while managing COVID-19 outbreaks in Washington State, Wisconsin, and Wisconsin's Milwaukee county. Ultimately, we conclude that health control strategies should prioritize the stabilization of the contact network at the lowest possible effective reproduction number ($R_t$) that avoids excessive hospital overload, a target that can be potentially achieved through vaccination.

Specifically, we analyze how, under appropriate dark-state conditions, the interaction between spin-exchange collisions and photoassociation facilitates the stable formation of atom-molecule pairs from three initial spin-zero atoms. This mechanism, involving two distinct two-body interactions, can be conceptually understood as an effective three-body recombination. We explore the respective influences of photoassociation and initial magnetization in the "resonant" scenario where the dark-state condition is perfectly met. Additionally, we investigate the "non-resonant" regime, where this condition is either approximately fulfilled (the adiabatic case) or not met at all. In the adiabatic scenario, we develop an effective non-rigid pendulum model that enables a clear discussion of the emergence of antiferromagnetic instability in an "atom-molecule pendulum," alongside phenomena such as large-amplitude pair oscillations and atom-molecule entanglement. Finally, we consider the extreme non-resonant case, illustrating how atom-molecule entanglement arises due to effective three-body recombination when the non-rigid pendulum emerges from a broad range of magnetization states. These findings on atom-molecule entanglement and magnetic properties may prove relevant for designs involving molecule-molecule entanglement or three-body recombination-like processes in systems with comparable interaction strengths. Overall, the non-resonant non-rigid pendulum serves as a universal archetype of atom-molecule entanglement within spin-1 Bose-Einstein condensates, provided the photoassociation rate is not negligibly small. This setup also resembles the Fermi-Hubbard model with next-nearest-neighbor interactions, potentially enabling atom-molecule entanglement through mechanisms like the Heisenberg spin chain or the emergence of large matter-calcite entanglement from maximum magnetization states. Along the way, we establish effective Hamiltonians that capture the essential physics of this system. Additionally, we discuss the feasibility of this proposal using current experimental techniques and highlight its potential generalizations to other systems with analogous microscopic interactions. The findings regarding the atom-molecule pendulum and its connected entanglement schemes are original contributions. While similar concepts have been explored in Refs. [48, 49], our work distinguishes itself by employing photoassociation rather than molecular mean fields, utilizing photoassociation to generate entangled atom-molecule pairs from spin-mixed BECs, and providing a detailed discussion on the feasibility of manipulating these states into heuristic Hubbard models with emerging correlations.

Successfully integrating these causal structures enhances a model's capacity to generate more robust and intelligible predictions. Because fields such as biology, social sciences, and health are dynamically changing, there is a critical need for time-sensitive causal models capable of accounting for external events and influences that affect phenomena across diverse domains and domains. However, existing causal discovery methods often struggle when applied to time-series data, a challenge exacerbated by the complex, stochastic, and high-dimensional nature of these datasets. These limitations have hindered the development of effective tools for uncovering causal relationships in fields like natural language processing (NLP) and economics. To address these issues, this review introduces a comprehensive taxonomy of discovery techniques, extending beyond standard frameworks to include modern methods for identifying exogenous shocks and their causal impacts. Additionally, we extend the traditional causal discovery process to encompass data pre-treatment, model discovery, and post-discovery evaluation. Finally, we present a detailed survey of recent advancements and their corresponding algorithms, offering insights and recommendations for future research directions in the domain of causal deep learning. This survey serves as a thorough overview of recent developments and algorithms for time-series causal learning, providing valuable perspectives and suggestions regarding upcoming trends in time-series causal discovery.

However, when normalizing to the same physical area, the bulge exhibits a more extended NUV$-r$ distribution and, in the most massive instances, is around 0.3 mag bluer than the average disc. This suggests that bulges in these galaxies are less quenched than their outer regions. Furthermore, bulge expansion produces two primary outcomes: first, the intrinsic bulge population becomes slightly younger; second, the overall NUV$-r$ increases due to a higher proportion of massive, short-lived O and OB stars per unit area. In summary, while bulge expansion does not significantly alter the B$^{<}$_500z$ MS for bulged galaxies with masses $<10^{11} M_{\odot}$, the effect is far from negligible at the lowest masses. The three most probable drivers of this elevation are enhanced star formation efficiency (SFE) in the bulge, the migration of old stars from the disc to the bulge, or a combination of these factors.

The RO-1001 bursts exhibit higher masses and charmass compared to other $z>2$ bursts, suggesting that major in-situ star formation is the primary driver of cosmic enrichment in the high-mass end of the stellar mass function during the quasar era. otonic radial rotation profile in a low-mass, low-luminosity giant star. While low- and intermediate-mass stars typically exhibit rigid rotation on the main sequence, stellar evolution into the giant phase—characterized by core contraction and envelope expansion—generally predicts a profile with a rapidly rotating core and a slower envelope and surface. KIC 9267654, however, displays a surface rotation rate exceeding that of its bulk envelope, contradicting standard angular momentum conservation expectations. We enhance the spectroscopic constraints on the surface rotation, confirm that pulsation frequencies align with previously determined core and envelope rotation rates, and establish that the star lacks significant chemical peculiarities. Furthermore, we evaluate evidence against the presence of a tidally interacting companion. Finally, we explore possible origins for this anomalous rotation profile, such as the accretion of a giant planet or anomalous angular momentum transport via tidal inertial waves driven by a close substellar companion, and advocate for additional observational and theoretical investigations. KIC 9267654 offers a unique opportunity to test theoretical models of angular momentum evolution in giant stars and their response to external perturbations. The presence of the weak fractional dissipation $\kappa\Lambda^{\alpha}u$ does not prevent blowup; it merely moderates it by extending the time required for the solution to reach singularity. This result addresses an open question previously raised in literature [2, 7]. The proof strategy involves reducing the problem to a differential inequality, a method that is broadly applicable to similar regularity spaces. During this process, we also derive a general blowup criterion.

Although graph neural networks (GNNs) are popular for modeling these structures, their capacity to represent simple, explainable laws governing dynamic behavior remains unverified. This study aims to discover and explain the interaction rules of time-varying networks using a simple mathematical framework. To achieve this, we introduced a two-step method: first, a differential equation-based approach identifies a target network structure and establishes an abstract metanetwork among nodes with simple interaction laws; second, the KNN-GNN algorithm reconstructs the time-varying network structure from the abstract representation's temporal evolution. Our findings from both synthetic and real-world data indicate that the network's temporal dynamics are governed by a community structure derived from the abstract metanetwork's interaction rules. Specifically, communities with high linkage strength in the abstract structure synchronize their activity, while isolated communities display random activity patterns. Furthermore, the duration of this activity synchronization is inversely proportional to the community partitioning cost of the abstract network. By revealing these principles, we established a novel and effective framework for explaining the dynamics of time-varying networks through their underlying simple interaction rules. Additionally, this approach offers a practical method for reconstructing time-varying network structures using the statistical properties of the abstract representation's activity dynamics. Finally, we propose an intermediate representation for these networks, facilitating more effective analysis via existing mathematical models and theoretical frameworks. Beyond its application to time-varying networks, this work also serves as a simple model for encoding network topology into the high-dimensional latent space of GNNs, reflecting the network's community structure. Consequently, various real-world networks can be decoded from their latent embeddings using community detection algorithms. The proposed method's utility is further highlighted by its ability to capture the network's time-evolutionary characteristics, which cannot be represented in latent spaces from independent node distributions. Overall, this research confirms that many real-world networks share the same simple interaction rules in their abstract structure, offering a new perspective on network "species" and their activity dynamics. We believe this result provides a novel and significant contribution to network science, particularly for explaining the dynamics of time-varying networks through simple interaction rules and for encoding network topology into latent spaces that reflect structural properties.

Deep learning has demonstrated remarkable success in various intelligent applications, particularly because end-to-end learning enables automatic feature extraction and optimization for downstream tasks like image classification. This approach is appealing because it relies on fundamental dynamics, thereby circumventing the invalid assumptions found in mass-flux convection schemes at current resolutions. Nevertheless, the optimal closure strategies for multi-fluid equations governing atmospheric convection remain unclear. This study develops a straightforward single-column model featuring two fluids—one rising and one falling—without incorporating additional sub-filter variability modeling. When applied to Rayleigh-Bénard convection, the model demonstrates that minimal closures suffice to predict the correct scaling of heat flux (Nu) across six orders of magnitude in buoyancy forcing (Ra). These findings indicate that even a rudimentary two-fluid model can effectively capture the primary coherent overturning structures of convection. Consequently, resolving these features in larger-scale models would likely enable the use of even more simplistic closures. Furthermore, this capability would empower researchers to investigate the emergence of other three-dimensional variations, including oscillatory instabilities and the secondary circulation known as the Reynolds cycle. Ultimately, the findings suggest that current efforts should focus on improving the resolution of resolving models to make them compatible with the most elementary closures for two-fluid dynamics.

The solar wind exhibits both temporal and spatial fluctuations in its properties, yet the mechanisms driving these variations remain incompletely understood. While MHD instabilities have been proposed to account for temporal changes, their role in spatial variations remains unconfirmed. This study employs a novel methodology to examine both temporal and spatial variations, utilizing a new 1.5-hour high-cadence magnetometer dataset from the Wind spacecraft covering one Earth rotation. Empirical models are utilized to identify and remove variations caused by the magnetosheath and bow shock, ensuring the analysis reflects true solar wind changes. The results reveal that most variability is concentrated in boundary layers rather than the core flow, suggesting that MHD instabilities operate more intensely in these regions. Furthermore, a previously unreported correlation is detected between the local time and a specific property of the solar wind: the ratio of right- to left-handed circularly polarized fluctuations near the ion cyclotron frequency. This implies the presence of a single type of instability, probably the ion cyclotron instability, throughout the entire Earth-orbit path. While this instability is most commonly associated with sub-sonic structures, they must therefore display spatial variations in a manner similar to other KHI-like structures.

We analyze the conditions required for these three uncorrelated atoms to achieve genuine multipartite entanglement. Our results indicate that this process is unattainable if the cavities interacting with the uncorrelated atoms share classical correlations with any other cavity. However, we observe that the atomic states can become genuinely multipartite entangled if the cavity housing the uncorrelated atom is highly entangled with another cavity. This non-trivial finding offers a potential method for generating multipartite entangled atoms through Jaynes-Cummings interactions and can be implemented using existing experimental setups. Furthermore, we propose an alternative approach to create these entangled states by employing a single cavity initially in a coherent state. This scheme involves a six-step protocol of Jaynes-Cummings interactions between the atoms and the field, achieving a fidelity of 0.99999 for a mean photon number of $n=10$. This proposal holds significance because the atomic Bell state is a fundamental resource for various quantum information tasks. Furthermore, this work underscores the capability of the Jaynes-Cummings model to generate multipartite entangled states from simple initial conditions without relying on cavity dissipation, a mechanism usually exploited to convert atomic states into entangled states within the Jaynes-Cummings framework.

A prevalent strategy to reduce bandwidth usage involves streaming only the portion of the video within the user's current viewport, a process that necessitates accurate viewpoint prediction. Current prediction approaches primarily focus on head movement trajectories and video saliency, yet they overlook navigation cues embedded within the video content. Viewpoint prediction remains a critical component for delivering high-quality 360-degree virtual tourism experiences; by leveraging subtitles for navigation, this work demonstrates that additional content can be effectively incorporated into viewport prediction frameworks. The proposed method represents a pioneering effort to exploit subtitles for viewport prediction in 360-degree video streaming and can be readily adapted to other video types, such as first-person games. Traditionally, this process requires access to both the training data and the teacher's internal parameters, a setup often impractical in real-world scenarios due to storage constraints or privacy concerns. To address this, we introduce Decision-Based Black-Box (DB3) knowledge distillation, which trains a student model using a black-box teacher that reveals only class labels instead of softmax probabilities. Our approach first addresses cases where training data is available: we calculate a sample's robustness against other classes by measuring its distance to the teacher's decision boundaries to generate soft labels for standard KD training. We further extend this method to scenarios where even training data access is impossible by generating pseudo-samples that are maximally distinguished by the teacher's decision boundaries, using their derived soft labels as a transfer set. Experiments across various benchmark networks and datasets confirm the effectiveness of our methods, with source code available at https://github.com/zhengjia94/DB3-KD.

### 1 Introduction

Deep learning has driven significant progress in fields such as computer vision, natural language processing, and speech recognition. However, the substantial computational costs of these sophisticated models often hinder their practical deployment. Knowledge distillation offers an effective solution by enabling a small student network to inherit the performance of a large teacher network. In standard KD frameworks, the teacher softens labels from one-hot vectors to high-capacity soft labels representing class distributions, which the student learns to predict, complementing the hard labels found in traditional supervision. Despite its success, conventional knowledge distillation remains limited by its reliance on white-box access to the teacher network.

In practical applications, black-box knowledge distillation has gained attention because the teacher may reside on a different server or be a proprietary system offering only class labels. Although existing research exists to bridge this gap, current black-box methods still struggle with high storage demands and data privacy issues. This paper focuses on accelerating deep networks via black-box knowledge distillation using a novel framework we call Decision-Based Black-Box (DB3) KD.

To address this limitation, this paper introduces a new framework named Co-Imitation Learning (CoIL), which utilizes an agent with even minimal skills to demonstrate only the most critical states required by the expert. Specifically, the skilled expert focuses on demonstrating states where it can generate significant policy improvements over the less capable agent, thereby reducing the costly demonstration process. Experimental results indicate that CoIL significantly outperforms state-of-the-art imitation learning methods. Additionally, we released the code for a novel, interactive toy environment featuring an animated expert and an agent to allow others to test CoIL. Finally, we extended the environment to include a continuous state space, demonstrating that CoIL remains effective even in this more complex setting. Using this proposed metric, PAC code decoding requires computational effort comparable to sequential decoding of conventional convolutional codes. Likelihood Estimation (MLE) pre-training is a flexible approach for boosting Neural Machine Translation (NMT) performance. Nevertheless, recent studies suggest that RL's benefits in NMT largely stem from reinforcing tokens that were already highly probable during pre-training. Consequently, we propose that RL's true potential in NMT remains untapped. To address this, we introduce "bold curriculum," a curriculum learning framework designed to strengthen RL's reinforcement of rare tokens. In this framework, we organize training into multiple progressive curricula, gradually increasing the difficulty of translation tasks. Specifically, we replace tokens at progressively harder positions within the target sequence during data creation. We implemented this bold curriculum strategy using (Multi-Objective) Reinforcement Learning (MOPO) as our objective model and observed significant gains in both English-to-German and Chinese-to-English translation tasks. When integrated with MOPO, our method yields an average of 0.52 more points in BLEU scores compared to baseline results. Furthermore, our findings indicate that this bold curriculum approach is largely transferable across various objective models, including single-objective models like Evolutionary Algorithms and other RL algorithms. Even when applied to randomly initialized objective models, the approach proves effective. During evaluation, both our bold curriculum strategy and the objective model contribute uniquely to overall performance. During the experimentation phase, the objective model demonstrated that MOPO successfully reinforced rare tokens, whereas traditional RL algorithms failed to do so. However, during the exploration stage, our results highlighted that the RL algorithms' performance suffered because the data was not sufficiently diversified. Consequently, we concluded that algorithms capable generating diverse sequences, such as Population Based Training (PBT), can effectively utilize this bold curriculum. Thus, PBT alongside our method achieves state-of-the-art performance in both English-to-German and Chinese-to-English translations. In summary, our contributions are threefold: (1) we demonstrated that RL algorithms can effectively reinforce rare tokens when paired with a bold curriculum; (2) we found that algorithms capable of producing diverse outputs are essential for the success of this approach; and (3 we proved that even randomly initialized objective models can benefit from this framework. Ultimately, our goal is to develop more powerful translation systems by creating a curriculum that gradually intensifies reinforcement on rare tokens.

This study experimentally investigates time-discrete, periodically driven dynamics in a single photon coupled to an environment. We present a comprehensive theoretical framework that elucidates the experimental findings and provides an analytical description of the system's non-equilibrium steady states. Furthermore, we show that both the periodic driving and environmental properties can be engineered to sustain an asymptotically non-vanishing bidirectional information flow between the open system and its environment. This approach relies on inducing limit cycle dynamics, which asymptotically trap information flow within a specific range of the environment coupled to the LHC. To address these challenges, we introduced MoDBO, a view maintenance system for MongoDB designed to handle recurrent data joins and frequent schema updates. MoDBO delivers two key features: (1) automated view maintenance for recurring joins and (2) efficient, non-invasive schema evolution. Evaluations using both synthetic datasets and three extensive real-world datasets demonstrate that MoDBO achieves up to six orders of magnitude faster performance for data joins compared to direct storage, and it is up to 2.6x faster than other systems during schema updates. Additionally, MoDBO supports multiple concurrent schema versions, enabling applications with inconsistent data sources. By supporting 250 GB datasets with 25% duplicate tuples across 18 partitions in under 20 minutes, MoDBO surpasses existing solutions. The source code and dataset are accessible at https://github.com/CMU-DB-Lab/ModBO. MongoDB is open source, allowing custom index creation and document schema modification; however, these capabilities are limited and result in suboptimal performance. MoDBO overcomes these limitations by facilitating efficient data joins and frequent schema updates. Unlike prior work, this approach exploits the database's native features to create structured indexes on source tables with distinct schemas. Specifically, MoDBO organizes these indexes as directed acyclic graphs (DAGs), supporting multiple concurrent schema versions. Furthermore, unlike other systems, MoDBO maintains high performance even with large datasets containing significant duplicate tuples.

This study explores the connectivity and geometry of cliques in 2-dimensional air resistance networks derived from historical data (historical periods: 1600s, 1800s, 1920s; geographic scope: Europe plus North and South America). Recent works have also detected similar 2-dimensional structures in other resisting systems, such as protein interactions and social media hashtags. Recent research has demonstrated the applicability of this approach to various systems of interacting entities.

Both approaches yield solutions with comparable properties that undergo qualitative shifts based on the adiabatic index $\gamma$ relative to critical values $\gamma_+ \approx 1.601$ and $\gamma_- \approx 1.225$. Within the range $\gamma_- < \gamma < \gamma_+$, two distinct families of strong shocks exist, differing in their self-similar structure and spatial distribution of thermodynamic parameters. This coexistence results from a subcritical Hopf bifurcation (at $\gamma_-$) and a homoclinic bifurcation (at $\gamma_+$). For weak shocks (where internal gas energy is negligible), two solutions are possible: one involving compression and the other expansion. As the shock strength increases, the admissible range for $\gamma$ narrows (bifurcation at $\gamma_-$) and eventually vanishes (bifurcation at $\gamma_+$). When $\gamma > \gamma_+$ or $\gamma < \gamma_-$, the system supports only a single strong shock solution, with the post-shock gas either failing to condense or expanding indefinitely. Additionally, the origin of the self-similar solution (whether at $r=0$ or $r=R_{sh}$) and the behavior of the analytic approximate solution are examined. The analytical findings align closely with the exact numerical results, validating the approach. This research elucidates the complete set of strong shock solutions across all spatial scales, from the shock front down to the origin. The bifurcations at $\gamma_-$ and $\gamma_+$ correspond to subcritical Hopf and homoclinic bifurcations, respectively—phenomena previously unreported in this context. These results have significant implications for astrophysical and cosmological phenomena, including supernova and gamma-ray burst explosions, planetary/meteorite core formation, and the explosive nucleosynthesis of light elements.

We construct a dynamic framework for distributing such opportunities within a society characterized by mobility bottlenecks, where optimal allocation involves balancing the immediate benefits to the current generation against the potential to uplift future generations' socioeconomic composition. Our analysis demonstrates that optimal allocations emerge from continuous optimization problems spanning multiple generations, revealing that these solutions often prioritize individuals from lower socioeconomic backgrounds over slightly more successful high-status peers—a form of affirmative action that arises organically from the pursuit of payoff maximization. Furthermore, we examine how model parameters influence whether this affirmative action is temporary or persistent, and we explore extensions incorporating more complex mechanisms governing transitions between socioeconomic levels. This research underscores how our dynamics-driven perspective highlights mechanisms for promoting generational mobility that may be overlooked in static analyses, while also providing actionable insights into designing access mechanisms that maximize both competitive performance and mobility. To achieve this, we introduce a dynamic prioritization algorithm and offer empirical support for its benefits using realistic simulation data. Access mechanisms based on this algorithm outperform alternative methods in experiments designed to measure payoffs across generations, and it significantly enhances intergenerational mobility when implemented in actual school admissions contexts.

Abstract/Description: This study investigates the impact of access mechanisms on both immediate performance and long-term socioeconomic mobility. While access mechanisms are typically optimized for immediate outcomes, we demonstrate that designing for generational effects can yield access systems that enhance mobility. Our dynamic priority network model underscores the importance of network structure in this process, a factor often neglected in existing literature. This approach highlights mechanisms for improving generational mobility that other models may miss, and we empirically validate these findings with a realistic experiment. Access mechanisms designed specifically to maximize intergenerational mobility surpass state-of-the-art methods in real-world school admissions. Access mechanisms we propose as alternative solutions maximize the sum of performance and mobility over two generations and can be readily adapted to contexts where extending beyond two generations is feasible. Access mechanisms we present are applicable to any setting possessing generational structures, such as contests granting life-long benefits to participants.

Access to higher education facilitates intergenerational mobility, allowing individuals to surpass their parents' socioeconomic status. This paper outlines a dynamic framework for allocating access opportunities across generations to maximize performance while considering such mobility. Despite this, current models often focus exclusively on immediate performance and ignore the issue of trapping individuals in certain socioeconomic states across generations. To address this, we developed an algorithm that optimizes access mechanisms based on a dynamic priority network, thereby promoting intergenerational mobility. We verify the mechanism's effectiveness in realistic experiments

Large Hadron Collider (LHC) implemented a novel rapid luminosity separation technique known as "Emittance Scans." These scans were executed systematically during every fill featuring full-intensity beams under physics production conditions at the Interaction Point (IP) of the Compact Muon Solenoid (CMS) experiment. This method enables the determination of both emittance and closed orbit parameters at the bunch-by-bunch level. By precisely measuring the beam-beam closed orbit discrepancies, researchers achieved a direct and quantitative observation of long-range beam-beam PACMAN effects, with results that align closely with numerical simulations generated by an enhanced version of the TRAIN code. Currently, data collected from these Emittance Scan operations at the LHC are being utilized to indirectly measure beam-beam parameters at the IP within the future High-Luminosity Linear Collider (ILC) at Jefferson Lab. At the ILC, this same technique will serve as a primary method for high-precision measurements of beam-beam emittance and closed orbit parameters at the IP. Furthermore, the ILC's superior beam quality, symmetric structure, and precise diagnostics offer significant advantages over the LHC environment. These measurements are expected to achieve a 1% precision for the beam-beam emittance and better than 10 micrometers for the closed orbit, representing improvements of two orders of magnitude and one order of magnitude, respectively, compared to current forward pipe emittance and closed orbit precisions at the ILC. These findings will be achieved despite minor perturbations introduced by diagnostic devices and the beam-breakup cavity. Additionally, the analysis will provide a more comprehensive description of the potential beam-beam parameter set at the ILC and offer a refined estimation of measurement precisions. This demonstrates that the Emittance Scan technique has evolved into a signature method for high-precision beam parameter determinations at the future linear collider.

Specifically, these malicious nodes divert the network from the optimal solution by transmitting deceptive data to their neighbors while consuming substantial communication bandwidth. We introduce a distributed gradient-based algorithm wherein benign agents exchange quantized information. We demonstrate that the solution converges to a neighborhood of the optimum and analyze the resulting solutions under communication constraints and the influence of malicious agents. Additionally, numerical simulations are provided to validate these findings. The proposed approach underscores the robustness of quantum communication channels against malicious behavior and highlights the significant reduction in bandwidth compared to real-valent communications.

In recent years, the rise of Internet-of-Things devices has fueled substantial growth in mobile data traffic, creating a urgent need for content caching at the network edge. A fundamental task in this context is determining which objects to cache and when, based on object popularity and temporal patterns. This results in a distributed time-series optimization problem where each node adapts its decisions using only local information. To address this, we propose a novel adaptive distributed algorithm. First, we establish that the ideal solution involves aggregating time-averaged functions of data processed by individual nodes. However, when nodes have time-varying delays in accessing this data, we show that the popular strongly convex time-series "Dual Averaging" methods fail to solve the problem optimally. Consequently, we introduce a new algorithm that leverages duality theory to design time-scales separating the slow adaptation needed for time-series data from the fast dynamics of dual updates. This results in a scheme where node decisions depend on data from a single time instant. Simulation results confirm that the proposed method outperforms existing algorithms both in constrained and convex optimization scenarios. Furthermore, unlike most current content caching strategies, this approach does not rely on estimates of object popularity.

Quantum key agreement enables two distant users to jointly generate an identical and secret key, a capability proven vital for various cryptographic applications. This paper introduces a time-efficient quantum key agreement protocol utilizing a discrete variable continuous quantum state. The protocol ensures that a key can only be formed if both users actively cooperate to establish it. Additionally, the scheme is resilient to channel noise and allows for the generation of a key bit per transmitted message. Numerical simulations validate these advantages, which also distinguish this work from other quantum key agreement protocols.

background (CMB) serves as a fundamental probe in physical cosmology. Due to the faintness of this signal, researchers have developed increasingly sophisticated and sensitive experiments that observe the sky across multiple frequencies using thousands of polarization-sensitive detectors. However, the high sensitivity of these instruments means that instrumental systematic effects can become the primary obstacle to fully exploiting their data. This paper introduces s4cmb (Systematics for CMB), a Python package designed to simulate time-domain raw data streams from modern bolometric CMB experiments while injecting realistic instrumental systematics. The package aims to evaluate contamination from these effects in real data, inform the design of future instruments, and enhance the realism of simulated datasets necessary for developing precise data analysis techniques. s4cmb builds upon the simcmb framework and systematics characterization methods outlined in prior publications [S. Tsai et al., Phys. Rev. D 100, 023012 (2019); S. Tsai et al., Phys. Rev. D 101, 083016 (2020); and S. Tsai et al., Phys. Rev. D 104, 083015 (2021)]. This work extends previous studies by investigating several additional systematic effects critical for high-sensitivity experiments, including non-Gaussian time-loading beam shapes, dipoles induced by Earth's rotation, and radiometric calibration uncertainties. These simulations are performed in the time domain for real measurements from observational datasets. Furthermore, this paper presents a forward model to calculate radiometric calibration uncertainties, offering a more precise evaluation method than traditional bandwidth-uncertainty estimates. This approach accounts for uncertainties arising from the blackbody radiation of a load, the cold sky, and the secondary atmosphere, as well as uncertainties in microwave vapor absorption. We provide a comprehensive guide to utilizing the forward model for estimating radiometric calibration uncertainties, which can be applied to any experiment with a dual-receiver setup capable of simultaneously measuring the load and cold sky. By employing the simcmb package, users can simulate raw time-domain streams from multi-receiver observational datasets that include multiple celestial sources and radio frequency interference (RFI). The simulated data incorporate realistic instrumental systematics, such as spatial and temporal beam patterns, gain and phase uncertainties, and receiver noise characteristics. Additionally, the package supports the inversion of these same observational datasets in the map domain to derive full-sky temperature and polarization (Stokes Q and U) maps, along with their respective uncertainty

Although prior research has employed linear models and neural networks for this purpose, the application of pre-trained language models remains unexplored, as does the rationale behind their utility. This study utilizes BART as a case study to demonstrate its efficacy in word ordering. Furthermore, we expand our analysis through probing techniques to empirically determine that syntactic dependency knowledge within BART serves as a robust explanation for its performance. Additionally, we document performance improvements achieved with BART in the related partial tree linearization task, which further validates our findings. Our open-source resources are accessible at https://www.sweetnonsense.com/sortingwords/.

Multilingual Natural Language Inference (NIL) facilitates the discovery of equivalent statements across numerous languages, proving valuable for diverse applications. This paper introduces "NIL aligner," a system dedicated to generating high-quality sentence pairs for human evaluation and the creation of multilingual coreference datasets. Our approach integrates a sentence encoder, a pair of BERT classifiers, and a curriculum learning framework. We achieve state-of-the-art results on five languages, with performance gains observed even in monolingual contexts. By employing probing methods, we demonstrate that multilingual lexical knowledge is essential for the system's success. Finally, we release a high-quality set of paired sentences across 103 languages, and our findings indicate that when incorporated into a simple NIL framework, this resource helps other systems achieve state-of-the-art performance. Our code and data are available at https://www.sweetnonsense.com/nil-aligner/.

This study investigates the application of preprocessing techniques for enhancing German text generation using character-level neural models. Specifically, we test a range of strategies, including subword segmentation, acoustic features, and acoustic feature dropout, across several generation tasks. Our results demonstrate that for word ordering, preprocessing offers no performance benefit and may be detrimental; conversely, in partial tree linearization, preprocessing yields improvements, particularly with acoustic feature dropout. These findings are documented in both English and German. Source code is available at https://www.sweetnonsense.com/partial-tree-linearization-.

Neural machine translation (NMT) has seen performance boosts from integrating linguistic knowledge such as morphology and syntax. However, accessing these resources across many languages remains difficult. This work proposes a novel approach to evaluate the semantic understanding of 250 languages by asking NMT systems to perform meaningful linguistic reordering tasks. We document that current open-source systems struggle to exceed chance levels on these tests. Our findings indicate that pretrained models

istic media across social networks has heightened the risk of widespread misinformation. Consequently, developing robust detection methods is urgent. This study introduces a new framework for distinguishing real from fake images and videos by training separate classifiers for various media types and subsequently fusing their decisions. For image classification, we adapt an existing state-of-the-art model after fine-tuning it on a balanced dataset comprising roughly 10,000 samples (5,000 real and 5,000 fake). To address the scarcity of video deepfake datasets, we constructed a balanced collection of deepfake videos featuring ten celebrity subjects using two generation techniques. We evaluated several recent video authentication approaches on this dataset to identify the most effective model for distinguishing deepfake videos from originals. Finally, we compiled a fused dataset to demonstrate the successful integration of real and fake media classifiers and to showcase the significant improvement in the overall system's accuracy. Since this is the initial attempt at creating a celebrity deepfake video dataset, no public benchmark exists for evaluating fake media detection. Consequently, we established a benchmark dataset and protocol to facilitate future research in this domain. Additionally, this study addresses several common misconceptions regarding deepfake generation and detection. The proposed methodology yields impressive results, achieving an accuracy of 98.50% on the celebrity deepfake video dataset and surpassing the state-of-the-art method on the image classification task. The source code for this project is accessible at this link: https://github.com/shreya2003/Deepfake-Detection.

Menger explored the concept of dimension by establishing an order on real-valued function $d$ defined on points $p$ of a topological space $X$, where $d(p_1, p_2, ... , p_{n+1})$ measures how far $n+1$ points $p_1, ..., p_{n+1} \in X$ are from lying in a plane. He demonstrated that a space $X$ is of dimension zero if and only it is discrete, and a space containing at most countable points is of dimension one precisely when Menger's function $d$ exists on those points such that for some $\epsilon > 0$, the condition $d(p_1, p_2) < \epsilon$ implies $\delta(p_1, p_2) < \epsilon$, where $\delta$ denotes a metric on $X$. This note demonstrates that if $d$ is a Menger's function on a countable topological space $X$ satisfying $d(p_1, p_2, p_3) \ge \min \{d(p_1, p_2), d(p_2, p_3), d(p_1, p_3)\}$ for all $p_1, p_2, p_3 \in X$, then $X$ possesses a topological dimension not exceeding one.

For a number field $K$ of degree $n$ with embeddings $\sigma_1, \dots, \sigma_n$ into $\mathbb{C}$, the norm is defined as $\lvert x \rvert = \sqrt{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \lvert \sigma_i(x)\rvert^2}$ for any $x \in K$. Under this norm, elements of $O_K$, the set of algebraic integers in $K$, correspond to points in $\mathbb{R}^n$ forming an arbitrary lattice. We examine the proportion of such lattices where the shortest non-zero vector has norm strictly less than 1. By applying Siegel's mass formula for classical groups, we find this proportion is exactly $\prod_{j=1}^n (1 - 1/p^j)$ when $p$ is the sole ramified prime of $O_K$, and it exceeds this product when there are multiple ramified primes. For quadratic fields ($n=2$), this proportion is equivalent to $\phi^*(O_K)/\psi^*(O_K)$, extending classical results by Minkowski and Cohen regarding units and integers with a given norm. In all these cases, the resulting expressions are smaller than $1 - 1/p$. We also determine the measure of fields where the norm of the generator with smallest absolute value is at most 1. These computations generalize Minkowski's bound, which asserts that every class in the ideal class group of $O_K$ contains an integer with norm at most $\frac{2}{\pi}\sqrt{\lvert D_K \rvert}$, where $D_K$ is the discriminant of $K$. Finally, we discuss implications for the first ideal class. An appendix by P. Stevenhagen addresses the case where $O_K$ possesses no units of norm $-1$.

group ${\bf U}_q(\mathfrak{g})$ for ADE-type Lie algebras. Specifically, we establish a natural Hopf algebra isomorphism between ${\bf U}_q(\mathfrak{g})$ and a quotient of the Weyl group invariants within the Fock-Goncharov quantum cluster algebra $\mathcal{O}_q(\mathscr{P}_{{\rm G},\odot})$. Utilizing the quantum duality of cluster algebras, we demonstrate that ${\bf U}_q(\mathfrak{g})$ possesses a natural basis $\bar{\bf \Theta}$ with structural coefficients belonging to $\mathbb{N}[q^{\frac{1}{2}}, q^{-\frac{1}{2}}]$. Furthermore, this basis $\bar{\bf \Theta}$ exhibits invariance under Lusztig's braid group action, Dynkin automorphisms, and the star anti-involution. As a consequence, we derive a new positivity property for the crystal basis of type $\mathfrak{g}$ associated with $\bar{\bf \Theta}$. Notably, our constructed $\bar{\bf \Theta}$ aligns with the Kripke-Berenstein-Littelmann-Ram-Shapira basis for type A and is linked to the canonical basis via a natural isomorphism. Additionally, we identify $\bar{\bf \Theta}$ with the geometric crystal basis defined by Frenkel and Reshetikhin for $\mathbf{U}_q(\mathfrak{g})$. This result yields a novel group-theoretic definition for the canonical basis of type $\mathfrak{g}$. In the specific case of type A, our definition of $\bar{\bf \Theta}$ reconciles the combinatorial constructions of Lusztig and Berenstein-Fomin-Zelevinsky. We also provide a comprehensive comparison of the quantum cluster algebra $\mathscr{P}_q(\mathscr{P}_{{\rm G},\odot})$ with the positive half of ${\bf U}_q(\mathfrak{g})$. Our approach generalizes the findings of Schiffrin (2018) and Shi (2018).

members of a hierarchical network generate profits by recruiting and exploiting a growing base of deceived newcomers. Although these schemes have operated for over a century, their precise mechanisms have remained undocumented and theoretically undefined, leaving them without a clear name or descriptive framework. This paper introduces a straightforward mathematical model of pyramid schemes that yields an explicit formula. The findings indicate that, unlike other network epidemics which typically follow an exponential growth curve until collapsing into a power law, pyramid schemes also evolve into power laws but achieve significantly larger final epidemic sizes. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that pyramid schemes constitute a specific subset of all possible epidemics characterized by a power law decay with an exponent of $\beta = 3$. Finally, the research explores how variations in the recruitment rule influence the power law exponent and outlines methods for generating non-pyramid pyramid-like schemes. These insights offer practical implications for understanding viral phenomena on social media, the structural formation of 3D polymer gels, and the generic properties of epidemics on hierarchical networks. The proposed simple model can also aid in analyzing other complex spreading processes, such as information diffusion, financial panics, and rumor propagation. Pyramids are defined as the sole epidemic type that maximizes both the power law exponent and the total size of a standard epidemic. This simple framework thereby provides insights into extreme events in power law distributions, self-similar structures in natural and artificial systems, and the mechanisms behind non-ergodic behavior.
