This study investigates 19 new GC candidates within the Galactic bulge by analyzing their near-infrared colour-magnitude diagrams (CMDs) derived from the VISTA Variables in the Via Lactea Survey (VVV) database. We determined key astrophysical properties for these objects, including reddening, extinction, distance, total luminosity, mean proper motions, metallicity, and age. To identify likely members, we applied a decontamination procedure to the sample using mean proper motion and extinction/expiration corrections on stellar photometry. The majority of the 19 candidates exhibit characteristics consistent with established bulge GCs, displaying CMDs that align well with simulation results regarding stellar population distribution. Furthermore, Poisson noise correction applied to the main sequence in the dereddened and extinction/expiration corrected CMDs reveals three new bulge GC candidates with distinct properties compared to the sample. These findings will significantly enhance our comprehension of the bulge GC population and facilitate the investigation of their association with stellar mass segregation. Specifically, when the network comprises a single type of tensor that also acts as an erasure correction code, we demonstrate that it is impossible to simultaneously achieve local contractibility and sustain power-law correlations. Driven by this no-go theorem and the necessity of local contractibility for efficient variational ansätze, we offer guidelines for designing networks with the single-tensor component that can support power-law correlations. Furthermore, we present an example of a network utilizing the single-tensor component that supports such correlations; this was previously introduced in the literature as the "entanglement (or Pyramix) network." Our results extend naturally to networks consisting of multiple distinct tensor types. Additionally, by connecting to the variational approach for the Hamiltonian of the 1D critical transverse field Ising model, we propose a novel network with the single-tensor component that supports power-law correlations and maintain local contractibility beyond its original scope. Overall, our findings assist in understanding the mechanisms underlying the emergence of critical phenomena within these networks and assist in creating networks with the single-tensor component capable of sustaining power-law correlations while remaining efficient ansätze. Our methods are general and apply broadly to various models featuring the Lee-Yang singularities.

Short-Term Memory (LSTM) models have proven effective in process mining, surpassing traditional methods in predictive performance. Building on this foundation, we evaluate four Graph Neural Network (GNN) variants alongside a dropout-enhanced fully connected Multi-layer Perceptron (MLP) to forecast the next activity's nature and timestamp. Unlike prior studies, we assess model efficacy across various process stages, segmented by quartiles of event counts and normalized case durations. This approach reveals that model behavior varies significantly throughout a business process. Notably, our experiments indicate that the straightforward MLP frequently outperforms more complex deep-learning architectures in both prediction tasks. Consequently, we emphasize the need for caution when deploying automated prediction techniques at different process phases and advocate for researchers to validate their findings against robust baselines such as simple MLPs. The source code from our experiment is openly accessible online.

It is established that the space ${\Sigma}^{\sigma}_s$ is nontrivial precisely when $s+ {\sigma} > 1$. We derive growth estimates for functions and their Fourier transforms within one-parameter spaces and provide characterizations based on short-time Fourier transform estimates for both these spaces and their duals. Furthermore, we identify the conditions on Toeplitz operator symbols required to ensure the continuity of these operators on one-parameter spaces. Finally, we demonstrate the applicability of our findings to the continuity of multiplication operators on one-parameter spaces. These results extend previous studies, which were limited to spaces where sub-exponential decay was solely imposed on the function or its Fourier transform. This line of research has various mathematical implications, including differential equations, Toeplitz operators, and $time$-$frequency$ analysis. This project was undertaken during the authors' visit to the International Centre for Theoretical Physics (ICTP), Abu Dhabi Campus. These data are vital for evaluating biosignatures in exoplanet atmospheres and calculating surface UV radiation doses for habitable zone planets orbiting low-mass stars. However, a significant constraint in these evaluations is the scarcity of near-ultraviolet spectral observations of such flares. To encourage further empirical study, we employed a grid of radiative-hydrodynamic simulations, incorporating an updated model for hydrogen line pressure broadening, to forecast the $\lambda \approx 1800-3300$ \AA\ continuum flux during the rise and peak of a well-documented superflare from the dM3e star AD Leo. These forecasts rely on semi-empirical combinations of radiative flux spectra, comprising a high-flux electron beam simulation with a substantial low-energy cutoff ($\gtrsim 85$ keV) and a lower-flux simulation with a smaller cutoff ($\lesssim 40$ keV). This two-component framework successfully accounts for hydrogen Balmer line broadening, optical continuum color temperature, Balmer jump magnitude, and the intensity and morphology of the far-ultraviolet continuum during the flare's rise and peak. Furthermore, by integrating spatially resolved analyses of solar flare data from the Interface Region Imaging Spectrograph with prior radiative-hydrodynamic models, we expanded these predictions to include electron flux spectra, He II $\lambda 304$ \AA\ emission, and UV continuum flux. These models are directly applicable to assessing atmospheric erosion and planetary habitability in terms of UV surface radiation for exoplanets near low-mass stars. Additionally, the electron flux spectra derived are consistent with those observed in solar flares that produced significant ionization and radiation belt populations. Radiative-hydrodynamic simulations of specific flaring events from active dMe stars, now aided by precise optical photometry, can yield electron flux spectra with narrower confidence intervals. These specifications are essential for interpreting far-ultraviolet spectrographs planned for near-term deployment, including the Swedish 1-m UV Solar Telescope, the Far Ultraviolet Spectroscopic Explorer, and the proposed NEAR-UV Emission Spectrograph for Habitable zone planets around M-dwarfs.

Nevertheless, point clouds possess two distinct characteristics that complicate learning and inference: data points lack inherent ordering, and systems must output ordered representations. Existing methods producing ordered outputs generally rely on iterative processes to generate predictions for individual points, which hinders their application to large-scale point cloud datasets. In this study, we introduce a dual tower framework that leverages global statistics and unlearned embeddings to perform simultaneous prediction for all points, enabling direct scaling to larger datasets. Since the model eliminates the need for sequential decoding, it can utilize any distance metric to order learned embeddings based on a reference point, ensuring that the predicted points maintain the same order as the input embeddings. Our approach is entirely non-recurrent and requires minimal hyperparameters. We benchmark the model across three diverse tasks and datasets: monochrome particle tracking (particle physics), star tracking (astronomy), and vehicle detection (autonomous driving). Experimental results demonstrate that the dual tower model surpasses current state-of-the-art methods and other dual encoder baselines. Furthermore, we provide a scalable analysis comparing the dual tower model with sequential models on point cloud datasets, confirming that our method scales efficiently from small datasets (approximately 100 samples) to very large datasets (exceeding 10 million samples). The dual tower model is open-source and readily adaptable to other tasks and datasets. The source code is accessible at: https://github.com/yzhang516/DualTower-PointCloud.

Large language models (LLMs) have shown remarkable success in natural language understanding and generation. Recently, researchers have attempted to adapt LLMs for 3D vision tasks, such as object detection and scene segmentation, by feeding them point clouds, camera intrinsics/extrinsics, and object hierarchies as input. However, these approaches often yield suboptimal results because many scenes contain irrelevant points and missing geometry, and the extensive parameter counts of LLMs make it challenging to encode complex visual data like point clouds. To address these issues, we present ReLMM: a new framework for efficient and accurate object detection using medium-scale vision models through multi-modal fusion. ReLMM employs lightweight networks to process point clouds, resulting in several optimized modalities with reduced dimensions that retain essential geometric information. These compact multi-modal features are then integrated into a vision-language model with heavily pruned object categories. Additionally, ReLMM incorporates a dynamic attention mechanism that adaptively selects the most informative points from each object's bounding box. Experimental results on the Waymo open

This approach successfully located poles corresponding to RPA excited states, including the electric dipole giant resonance in $^{16}$O. While the giant resonance is traditionally characterized as a single state with significant strength and width, the RPA analysis reveals that it actually consists of multiple distinct poles. Each of these poles possesses unique widths, origins, responses to residual interactions, and density fluctuation component structures. Furthermore, this study demonstrates that Landau damping serves as a primary mechanism for generating the width of RPA excited states, a finding with significant implications for dynamics in nuclear reactions and other many-body systems. To achieve these results, we developed a contour-bending technique to navigate poles through the complex energy plane as the screening parameter is altered; this method is broadly applicable to locating poles in the complex energy plane across various theoretical approaches. These capabilities are invaluable for comprehensively analyzing RPA excited states, which encode rich and nuanced physical phenomena. Consequently, this work provides a foundational approach for future investigations into collective modes, decay processes of excited states, and impurity behaviors using RPA or similar methodologies.

In many of these contexts, the underlying systems are dynamic, and due to their inherent complexity, constructing mathematical models suitable for clustering is often unfeasible. Furthermore, effective clustering of dynamic systems must explicitly account for their temporal evolution. This paper introduces a novel methodology for clustering dynamic systems directly from time-series data, inherently capturing the system's dynamical behavior. Specifically, we define a distance or similarity metric between system states based on their mutual influence, utilizing this measure for clustering. To enable data-driven computation, we employ the Koopman operator framework, which accommodates system nonlinearities, thereby extending the approach's applicability to diverse domains. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method by clustering three distinct dynamic systems: a linear system serving as a proof of concept, the highly nonlinear IEEE 39-bus transmission network, and dynamic variables derived from atmospheric data across the Amazon rainforest. Finally, we discuss the broader implications of this methodology for other areas of interest.

A primary reason for this failure lies in the fact that the discriminator, or classifier, tends to converge ahead of the generator, causing the gradient signals received by the generator to vanish. To address this issue, we introduce a simple yet potent retraining strategy that leverages a head start for the classifier. When applied, our method achieves generation speeds comparable to standard GANs while significantly surpassing current state-of-the-art models in terms of PPL and CTR metrics.

We investigate the role of large asteroids and comets as ejecta in planet-planet and planet-star interactions, respectively. Through hydrodynamic simulations, we show that planet-planet collisions can reach ejecta velocities sufficient for star-system escape, with the fastest planetesines originating from the collision between the secondary impactor and the main planet. The total mass capable of escaping varies significantly, from 10^-9 to 10^-3 times the mass of the impactor, relying on factors including the bodies' internal structures, collision velocity, and angle. For planet-star collisions, we simulate a range of impactor masses (10 to 10^4 Earth masses) and collision speeds, covering sub-sonic to supersonic regimes. We derive analytic expressions for the mass of escaping planetesines across these scenarios and validate them with additional simulations. The maximum escaping mass for planet-star collisions can exceed that of planet-planet collisions by nine orders of magnitude. However, while comets from planet-planet collisions arrive at targeted systems within 10 to 10^2 million years—allowing for in situ survival, potentially via dormant states those from planet-star collisions take too long to arrive to be viable. Consequently, the most probable source system for life in our Solar System is Proxima Centauri, the sole other star close enough to permit comet survival upon arrival. Furthermore, we identify a band of stars surrounding the Sun that could serve as life sources, assuming the mechanism exists. These band's location is determined by the orbit-period dependence of planetesimal ejection velocity and the survival time of comets upon entering new systems. Life from any star within this band is theoretically possible to deliver, but the most probable source is the closest star to us: Proxima Centauri.

A parallel statistical approach involves point process models, especially when points represent centroids rather than precise locations. This paper explores the connection between RSF and point process intensity, revealing that the standard logistic regression model for binary data serves as a Kiefer-Rosenblatt (KR) model for point processes. This model was originally developed to create minimally informative priors for Bayesian nonparametric density estimation via Dirichlet process mixtures. We demonstrate that the standard logistic model yields a KR prior with the same degrees of freedom used in Bayesian nonparametric density estimation. Furthermore, within a Bayesian framework, the posterior of the unknown selection function is proportional to the posterior of the unknown density. These findings indicate a close relationship among RSF, point processes, and Bayesian nonparametric density estimation. Additionally, an approximate method is proposed for estimating the Bayesian posterior of a selection function using thinning, a standard technique for sampling from Poisson point process realizations conditioned on a fixed number of points. Simulation results assess the method's performance and compare Bayesian estimates of selection functions across different approaches. The proposed technique offers advantages over existing methods when observations are unordered and only coordinates (not bearings) are available. This work is collaborative with T. Langlais.

While this method offers a more realistic and comprehensive representation compared to single-layer networks, it simultaneously introduces inherent complexities in system analysis. In this work, we present a method to study Kuramoto oscillators on multilayer networks by utilizing the join of matrices that encode both intra-layer and inter-layer connections. This strategy yields a "reduced" representation of the original multilayer system that exhibits equivalent dynamics. By solving for the reduced system and propagating these solutions back to the full network, we can determine system states. Furthermore, applying this same principle allows us to assess the stability of these states; by examining the Jacobian of the reduced system, we can derive insights into the Jacobian of the original multilayer network. This approach enables us to conclude that a state is unstable in the multilayer system if it is unstable in its reduced counterpart, and conversely, that stability in the reduced system implies stability in the full network. To demonstrate the broad applicability of this framework, we also investigated the impact of asymmetric and time-dependent couplings across layers. Our findings reveal that although these factors can establish the instability of a state in the reduced system (leading to instability in the multilayer system), they do not preclude the possibility of stability in the original multilayer network if the reduced system remains stable. Our results and conclusions are directly applicable to any connection scheme and can be generalized to other systems governed by first-order differential equations.

Consequently, there has been significant research into fast, approximate iterative methods for matrix inversion accelerated by Graphics Processing Units (GPUs). Concurrently, techniques for factoring sparse matrices have gained efficiency and accessibility through highly optimized software like SuperLU, MUMMAPO3, and givens-based approaches in packages such as MATLAB's `sparsei`. Despite these developments, the speed of resulting inverse matrices for specific applications remains unclear, particularly in contrast to applications using original system matrices. This study examines the performance and accuracy of algorithms from these leading packages aimed at computing inverses for large-scale sparse linear systems. We compare their performance against state-of-the-art applications utilizing the derived inverse matrices. Furthermore, we investigate how numerical precision impacts both computation time and memory usage across various packages. The findings offer practical insights for selecting appropriate algorithms and system solvers based on precision requirements, matrix characteristics, and available computational resources. To support these conclusions, we present empirical results from applications using the computed inverse matrices. Ultimately, our analysis reveals that despite advancements in iterative methods, direct methods capable of calculating matrix inverses remain highly effective. For instance, using a system solver (capable of solving Ax=b) approximately 10 times faster than application start-up times yields an application that is 1.5 to 2 times faster than using a pre-calculated inverse matrix. Additionally, storing more than one billion integers in half-precision format can lead to application speeds up to four times faster than when using single-precision format. Although high-precision formats increase memory consumption and potentially decrease computation time by roughly 10%, even with increased storage, this approach remains viable for many scenarios. Our results also highlight that modern GPU architectures can execute direct methods for matrix inversion up to 10 times faster than achieving a specific iterative convergence criterion.

In this study, we investigate the topological and localization characteristics of a one-dimensional Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model featuring spatially correlated random binary disorder. Our findings reveal that such binary disorder can trigger a transition from a trivial insulator to a topological Anderson insulator across multiple parameter regimes. These topological Anderson insulators are identified by a disorder-averaged winding number and localized bulk states, observable via the inverse participation ratio in both real and momentum spaces. Furthermore, the boundaries of the topological phases align with analytical predictions derived from the self-consistent Born approximation and the localization length. We also examine the impact of bimodal probability distributions on topological signatures and demonstrate that topological winding numbers can be reconstructed from correlation functions of real-space and momentum-space bulk states. Ultimately, this work extends the concept of topological Anderson insulators to disordered systems with binary probability distributions. The results presented here may assist in discovering and characterizing topological phases within binary-annealed quantum links and other experimentally realizable models. The source code for the simulations reported in this paper is available online. The topological signatures of the topological Anderson insulator, observed through localization lengths and inverse participation ratios in both real and momentum spaces, underscore the feasibility of engineering topological phases using binary-annealed quantum links with parameters that are experimentally accessible. While the study focuses on a one-dimensional chain, the findings can be generalized to higher-dimensional lattices, as the topological winding number can be extended to two dimensions through the construction of a topological crystalline Cartan index. Although this paper concentrates on the one-dimensional case, the underlying mechanisms and principles applicable to binary-annealed systems can be extended to higher-dimensional models.

Annealing involves slowly varying Hamiltonian parameters to explore equilibrium phases, making it a powerful method for solving complex optimization tasks. Conversely, quenches entail sudden Hamiltonian changes that drive the system into a non-equilibrium state. This study examines the connection between these two approaches, demonstrating that the critical bottleneck of quantum annealing—the minimum of the annealing gap—can be identified through a dynamical quench parameter characterizing the post-quench quantum state. By integrating statistical methods, such as neural network training, with quench data, we can reconstruct the complete functional behavior of the annealing gap. We further show that insights gained regarding the annealing gap, either partially or fully, enable the design of optimized quantum annealing protocols, yielding practical improvements in time-to-solution. These findings are based on simulations of random Ising Hamiltonians, which model challenging instances of the exact cover problem. Our results indicate that for certain instances, the current annealing gap estimate from D-Wave systems could be refined up to tenfold, or even more with additional data. Moreover, our approach offers a general framework for enhancing quench-based annealing gap estimates and does not depend on the specific structure of the Ising Hamiltonian. We also discuss the feasibility of these strategies on actual quantum hardware. Ultimately, our ability to significantly improve estimates of the annealing gap—without needing to know their exact values—provides a robust tool for evaluating and tuning quench-based eigenstate preparation schemes and other post-annealing protocols, such as reverse annealing and intermediate embedding.

We establish a Liouville theorem without relying on gradient estimates, demonstrating that any bounded harmonic function must be constant on such solitons. As a consequence, we prove that the dimension of the space of harmonic functions exhibiting polynomial growth is finite. Furthermore, we show that any harmonic function growing at most polynomially along the gradient of the potential undergoes asymptotically uniform convergence to a constant. Additionally, we obtain a compactness property for sequences of shrinking Ricci solitons that converge smoothly on compact manifolds and share a bounded dimension of harmonic functions with polynomial growth; specifically, any sequence with this property contains a subsequence that converges strongly. This compactness outcome implies the existence of a Ricci soliton within every connected component of the moduli space associated with shrinking Ricci solitons. a service has introduced new attack vectors, specifically backdoor attacks. These attacks conceal a secret function within a neural network that activates only when a specific trigger is present in the input. While most existing literature assumes static triggers with fixed locations and patterns—properties upon which many detection mechanisms rely—recent studies have demonstrated that image classification countermeasures like Neural Cleanse and ABS can be circumvented using dynamic triggers that remain effective regardless of their position or appearance. However, such dynamic backdoors are resource-intensive, typically requiring a significant portion of poisoned training data. This work presents the first demonstration that dynamic backdoor attacks can be executed on a per-sample basis. We introduce two approaches: the Gradient Method and the Optimization Method. Our experiments on image and natural language processing (SNL) classification confirm that these attacks can bypass recent detection systems, including Neural Cleanse, TDA, and FEDA. Furthermore, we investigate the feasibility of applying these attacks to text classification and highlight several distinct challenges and limitations compared to image-based scenarios. In summary, our contributions are threefold: (1) we show that current backdoor attacks can target recent detection countermeasures in text classification; (2) we expose unique difficulties and constraints when implementing image-based dynamic backdoors in text; and (3) we document the differences and challenges between executing dynamic backdoors on images versus text. This research underscores the urgent need for detection methods capable of identifying static backdoors in SNL classification. Our code is available at https://github.com/hillel-8/DynamicBackdoorAttack.

Among these effects, the post-Newtonian parameter $\gamma$, which quantifies gravitational light deflection, significantly influences astrometric data. This study analytically and numerically investigates how deviations of $\gamma$ from its general relativity value of unity impact parallax measurements in Gaia-like systems. Analytical calculations determine the shifts in parallax induced by deviations in $\gamma$, while numerical simulations employ Monte Carlo methods to model the parallax as a function of this PPN parameter. These simulations account for all data reduction steps in a astrometric pipeline, including data reduction, model fitting, and noise propagation. The results indicate a parallax deviation of approximately $1.35~\mu\text{as}$ for a source at mean squared displacement $\overline{r^2}=1\,\text{AU}^2$, corresponding to a relative error of $0.68\,\text{ppm}$, which exceeds the single-epoch precision of Gaia sources. Although this level of precision might suggest the need to account for $\gamma$ deviations in analyzing the brightest Gaia catalog, the actual precision is likely superior because unknown deviations in $\gamma$ would manifest as a systematic shift in parallax that can be identified and corrected using a subset of catalog sources with astrometric nebular references. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that the influence of $\gamma$ on parallax is not uniform across the Gaia field of view and can be empirically determined by assuming $\gamma$ is constant everywhere. Ultimately, this work reinforces the conclusion that the PPN parameter $\gamma$ can be determined to a precision better than $10^{-5}$ using Gaia-like data. Finally, the analytical expressions derived here may prove useful in interpreting the increasing precision of astrometric observations from next-generation missions such as The Surveyor or Euclid.

A significant hurdle in FL is the communication bottleneck between nodes and the PS. Although performing multiple local updates per iteration before syncing with the PS is a common strategy to alleviate this bottleneck, the statistical heterogeneity of node-specific data often results in biased models and delayed convergence. To overcome both communication and data heterogeneity issues, we investigate Random Walk (RW) learning algorithms. These algorithms utilize direct connections between nodes, which are typically more efficient than communicating with the PS. In this framework, the model acts as a "baton" passed iteratively to a neighboring node after each update. Designing effective RW algorithms is complicated by data heterogeneity and uncertainty regarding data distributions; specifically, ideally, each node should possess sufficient and representative data for model training. To manage these complexities, we propose a general stochastic (or "sample split") data distribution model that remains broad enough to encompass common practical scenarios, such as independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) data, clustered data, and linearly separable data. Based on this model, we evaluate standard RW algorithms, including ring-based and tree-based structures, demonstrating their convergence rates and conditions. Furthermore, we introduce a novel node-sampling alternating random walk algorithm that achieves the optimal $O(1/T)$ stochastic complexity. This is accomplished by sampling nodes proportionally to the square root of their data sizes, an approach that also yields an optimal $O(1/T)$ complexity for Riemannian data distributions. Finally, we provide an accompanying link containing the full source code for this algorithm. Our findings offer a comprehensive understanding of random walk algorithms' performance under data heterogeneity, potentially guiding the design of future protocols for large-scale learning systems. These methods depend on hand-crafted statistical and time-frequency features extracted from EEG signals. Although effective, this dependency represents a limitation. This paper introduces a convolutional neural network (CNN) model designed to classify epileptic seizures using EEG data that requires minimal manual preprocessing. The proposed architecture achieves this with two key objectives: (1) achieving state-of-the-art accuracy in distinguishing between patients with epilepsy and healthy individuals, and (2) accurately classifying seizure types (interictal, pre-ictal, and ictal) in patients with epilepsy. The model is trained on multichannel EEG data from only 10 patients with labeled EEGs and generalizes well to unseen testing datasets without any data augmentation. The objective is to estimate $E_G(\eta(\theta)) \equiv \eta_G$ using independent observations $Y_1, \dots, Y_n$, given that $Y_i \sim f(y|\theta_i)$ and $\theta_i \sim G$ are independent and identically distributed. Transfer learning has been suggested to address these challenges, even when bridging language gaps, such as adapting an English model for German ASR. In this study, we explore transferring an English model to Czech ASR, a task involving languages with lower mutual intelligibility. Our primary objective is to determine if mechanisms exist that guarantee the existence of pure Nash equilibria for every scenario while simultaneously ensuring fairness in the resulting allocations. Specifically, we investigate two relaxations of envy-freeness: envy-freeness up to one good (EF1) and envy-freeness up to any good (EFX), ultimately providing an affirmative answer. We present two mechanisms that exist in all universums, for which we prove the existence of pure Nash equilibria in weakly acyclic (WA) and log-superstable (LS) manners, which yield allocations that are respectively EF1 and EFX. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these mechanisms do not favor rich or poor agents. This is the first time such a broad range of fairness and efficiency properties has been simultaneously established. Additionally, we show that these mechanisms satisfy strong group strategyproofness (SPG) and (SPG) with a slight relaxation, as well as spg with logarithmic regret. To our knowledge, this also represents the inaugural demonstration that indivisible items can be allocated via a mechanism achieving EF1 or EFX while avoiding rich and poor outcomes, without any form of SPG. Our findings complement previous research on the topic. The key innovations of this work lie in the development of a novel potential function and a new analysis of the greedy best fit (GBF) algorithm. These techniques advance our understanding of the fairness and efficiency of the WA and LS equilibria for indivisible item allocations and have broader applications beyond this specific problem. We affirmatively answer the question posed by Procaccia and Wang (2050) regarding the EF1 and rich outcomes of GBF, and also address open questions from Haas et al. 839 exhibits a central region dominated by a nuclear starburst. By subtracting this starburst from the inner areas, residual surface brightness images and spectra were obtained from the outer spiral arms. The arms display distinct HII regions, which were targeted for spectroscopic observation using the 4.2-m William Herschel Telescope. These data were used to determine the physical properties of 28 HII regions, including their locations, luminosities, masses, and ages. By comparing these properties across the arms, the local angular rotation rate of the galaxy was derived. This rate was then fitted to a flat rotation curve model to identify the total dark matter content within one effective radius (Re), amounting to 3.0 x 10^9 Msun. Furthermore, the evolution of the half-light radius with stellar mass was analyzed to calculate the dark matter fraction within Re, showing it increases from 65% to 95% as the radius grows from 0.5 Re to 3 Re. These findings are consistent with other external spiral galaxies and imply that the dark matter profile transitions from an isothermal one at small radii to a profile with a finite central density at larger radii. Additionally, the presence of HII regions in the spiral arms indicates that this feature arises from local instabilities rather than the winding up of pre-existing spurs. Finally, the slight outward offset of the HII regions suggests that the one-armed spiral is not an intrinsic feature but a response to an external perturbation, most likely a companion object with a mass between 1.0 and 3.0 x 10^8 Msun located less than 1.3 kpc from the galaxy. UGC 8839 thus offers fresh insights into the origins of grand design spirals and the associated dark matter characteristics.

analyzing how mass accretion rates correlate with stellar and disk characteristics. While the scatter in these relationships can refine disk evolution models, this is only possible if accretion variability is properly accounted for. Although variability is significant during the embedded phases of star formation, it is often assumed to be minor in later stages. In this study, we report substantial accretion rate variations observed in the target XX Cha across multiple observations. These variations, which can alter by an order of magnitude between observations separated by as little as 1.5 years, suggest that statistical inferences about XX Cha's evolution may be skewed if this variability is ignored. This is the first time such significant accretion fluctuations have been documented for XX Cha; similar effects are likely prevalent in other systems. We suggest that future studies investigating XX Cha and similar objects must account for significant accretion rate variability to ensure that inferred distributions of disk properties remain unbiased.

However, practical applications often involve behavior policies generating joint trajectories with varying performance levels; for instance, one agent might follow a random policy while others adhere to medium-quality policies. In cooperative games with global rewards, existing offline MARL approaches often allow agents to inherit these suboptimal random policies, thereby compromising the team's overall performance. This paper investigates offline MARL with explicit attention to the diversity of individual agent trajectories and introduces a novel framework termed Shared Individual Trajectories (SIT) to mitigate this issue. Specifically, an attention-based reward decomposition network utilizes a differentiable key-value memory mechanism to assign credit to each agent in an offline setting. These decomposed credits facilitate the reconstruction of joint offline datasets into prioritized experience replay based on individual trajectories, enabling agents to share high-quality experiences. Subsequently, agents conservatively train their policies using a graph attention network (GAT)-based critic. Evaluations across discrete control environments (StarCraft II and multi-agent particle environments) and continuous control settings (multi-agent MuJoCo) demonstrate that our method yields significantly superior results on complex, mixed offline multi-agent datasets, particularly when there are substantial disparities in the quality of individual trajectories. Furthermore, we open-sourced both the multi-agent StarCraft II dataset and our codebase to further advance research in offline multi-agent learning. The experiment scripts for the multi-agent particle environment and multi-agent MuJoCo can be found at this link. Our approach represents an upgrade over prior offline multi-agent learning methods regarding the quality of individual trajectories and offers significant practical value. We hope this work incentivizes further efforts to develop higher-quality single-agent replay buffers in real-world applications and that our high-fidelity multi-agent StarCraft II dataset and privacy-preserving framework provide a robust foundation for additional experiments.

conference, Einstein proposed a thought experiment aimed at demonstrating the incompleteness of quantum mechanics by leveraging the instantaneous nonlocal collapse of the wave function—a phenomenon he termed "spooky action at a distance." In 1965, Bell formulated his famous inequality to provide quantitative support for the nonlocal nature of quantum mechanics, sparking intense debate that continues to this day regarding whether nature is inherently nonlocal or if the collapse of the wave function is illusory. Now, we demonstrate experimentally—building on our earlier work—at significantly enhanced levels of nonlocality that the counterfactual nature of wave function collapse can be bypassed in space-like separated events. This result directly contradicts local hidden variable theories, extends the nonlocality originally identified by Bell and Einstein beyond its initial bounds, and offers a visually intuitive proof of such nonlocality. Furthermore, our experiment confirms the "spookiness" first highlighted by Einstein and Bell in a real-world setting. The implications of our findings are directly applicable to emerging quantum technologies based on nonlocality, such as quantum cryptography, teleportation, and computation. The experimental setup involves sending photons through interconnected interferometric networks, utilizing the most straightforward version of Bell's inequality to achieve the strongest nonlocal effects ever recorded. This work represents the fifth most cited paper in the field of quantum optics since its publication in 2013.

advanced information technology systems has delivered substantial benefits to Internet of Vehicles (IoV) ecosystems, it has simultaneously amplified security and privacy risks. Consequently, privacy preservation methods have become a focal point in academic research to safeguard IoV data. However, these existing approaches require specific adaptations to align with actual IoV environments. Meanwhile, Federated Learning (FL) has emerged as a promising technique for enhancing both privacy and data utility within IoVs. Concurrently, Blockchain technology offers significant advantages through its decentralized and transparent storage mechanisms for data utility and access. This paper provides a comprehensive survey on the application of Blockchain-Enabled Federated Learning frameworks for data utility and access in IoVs. Notably, V392 Per demonstrates gamma-ray emission approximately 500 days after the initial spike, along with sustained nuclear fusion and active mass accretion. During the offline stage, the base station (BS) fits a GMM to uplink (UL) training data and subsequently generates a codebook in an unsupervised fashion by leveraging the model's clustering properties, assigning one codebook entry to each GMM component. In the online phase, the BS offloads the GMM to the mobile terminal (MT) without transferring the codebook; the MT then uses the GMM to identify the most appropriate codebook entry. This process eliminates the need for channel estimation at the MT, as it relies on the observed signal to calculate the responsibility of each GMM component. The feedback transmitted to the BS comprises the index of the component with the highest responsibility. Consequently, the BS combines the uplink training data with the selected codebook entry to establish a virtual beamformer for communication. Crucially, this approach requires no feedback transmission except for the GMM-based index. To our knowledge, this is the first GMM-based method that independently handles codebook generation (offline) and feedback selection (online). Simulation results indicate that the proposed approach significantly outperforms conventional methods. Furthermore, this framework is applicable to Type-1 codebooks.

We present a framework to achieve these currents on a cubic three-dimensional (3D) lattice featuring a Hofstadter model connected to two heat baths at distinct temperatures. Our results demonstrate that these currents possess dissipative robustness, maintaining stability despite impurities and gauge field tilting within specific nonequilibrium states. Furthermore, we identify protected boundary currents with authentic 3D robustness, meaning their stability relies on tunnelling occurring across all three spatial dimensions. The model also supports generic surface currents that remain robust in both bosonic and fermionic systems. Finally, we uncover the qualitative mechanism driving the robustness of these surface currents and highlight the pivotal influence of specific discrete symmetries. Beyond their intrinsic significance, these findings offer a straightforward method for engineering surface currents in thin-film materials and provide a straightforward experimental protocol to verify their robustness. Furthermore, this work establishes a simple mechanism for the robustness of surface currents within the iconic "desktop" 3D Hofstadter model, facilitating direct comparison with recent experimental observations. This mechanism operates through a 3D extension of the mechanism responsible for robustness in 2D surface currents on the same Hofstadter lattice, a mechanism first identified in our earlier publication [Phys. Rev. Lett. 124, 096803, 2020]. However, that earlier mechanism requires spatial modulation of the local magnetic field to ensure robustness, whereas the new mechanism described here achieves robustness in uniformly magnetized regions. Additionally, the mechanism operates via a distinct topological index and remains effective even in the quantum Hall insulator phase of the Hofstadter model. We believe this represents a fundamentally new mechanism for the robustness of surface currents, distinct from the previously known case involving spatial modulation of the magnetic field.

investigate Population III (Pop III) binary remnant mergers within nuclear star clusters (NSCs) during the early stages of structure formation. We track the dynamical evolution of Pop III compact object binaries as cosmic structures develop, calculating how field stars' dynamical friction drives these remnants into NSCs. Subsequent evolution inside the clusters is modeled through three-body interactions and gravitational-wave (GW) emission. Our results indicate that 7.5% of Pop III binary remnants will migrate to the galactic centers (within 3 pc). Of these, approximately 5–10% (around 500 per millisecond galaxy) will three-body scatter to super-relativistic velocities ($\sim$1–5 $v_c$), ejecting black hole (BH)-X-ray star (XS) or XS-BH pairs from their host galaxies. These fast mergers bypass the 3-nanosecond delay imposed by the GW waveform overlap region, leaving observable high-redshift ($z \gtrsim 10$) gravitational waves from scattered pairs that have avoided this constraint. Furthermore, a significant fraction of BH-BH pairs failing to scatter will still merge by $z \lesssim 1$, contributing substantially to the merger rate observed by LIGO/Virgo/KAGRA. This scenario offers a mechanism for producing the most massive merging mergers, including the potential candidate CMSCG1205-0100 with $36^{+9}_{-8} M_{\odot}$. Furthermore, X-ray surveys can observe the full sample of scattered mergers from local to high-redshifts ($z \sim 6$), providing constraints on Pop III XS formation, their dynamical evolution, and the mergers of the most massive black holes. This complements limits derived from GW detections and those set by the smallest accreted nuclei in present-day galaxies. Finally, the most fast-scattered systems may be ejected from galaxies, potentially seeding mergers in galaxy clusters at high-redshifts and establishing the initial conditions for supermassive black hole growth. This study directly addresses the physical processes governing the fate of Pop III binary remnants from their creation to post-merger ejection, offering estimates for each stage's contribution. Additionally, we present the time-dependent spatial distribution of these remnants to inform future detections by X-ray surveys and the Roman/Euclid telescopes.

Initially, the study focuses on a single-user, single-relay configuration, addressing a joint power optimization problem at the source and relay under individual power constraints for both nodes, with the goal of maximizing the end-to-end secrecy rate through optimal power allocation across subcarriers. Subsequently, the research expands to a more complex multi-user, multi-relay scenario. Utilizing a high signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) approximation for the end-to-end secrecy rate, an optimization problem is defined to jointly optimize power allocation at the base station, relay selection, subcarrier assignment to users, and power loading at each relay node. The objective is to enhance overall system security while adhering to independent power budget limits at each transmitter and exclusive subcarrier allocation to specific users. A joint optimization solution is derived for the simplified problem involving base station power loading and relay selection. Furthermore, closed-form solutions are obtained for the remaining optimizations of subcarrier assignment and power loading at the relays, respectively. Numerical results demonstrate that the proposed optimized schemes outperform existing optimization methods found in related literature. Overall, the proposed scheme for maximizing end-to-end secrecy rate extends from a multi-user, single-relay setup to a comprehensive multi-user, multi-relay environment by integrating subcarrier allocation, power loading at relays, and relay selection alongside independent per-node power constraints. Additionally, the high SNR end-to-end secrecy rate approximation employed in this work for multi-user, multi-relay OFDM systems can be applied to other contexts, such as single-user, single-relay or multi-user, single-relay systems, to optimize overall system throughput subject to independent power constraints across transmitters. In the contemporary context of escalating security concerns and privacy issues, the proposed optimized end-to-end secrecy rate scheme offers a robust solution for securing communications within multi-user, multi-relay OFDM frameworks. However, it is noted that the scheme for joint optimization of subcarrier allocation, power loading at relays, and relay selection remains for the users.

However, existing systems are hindered by slow performance, limited to roughly 300 steps per second, primarily because of outdated infrastructure. We introduce TextWorldExpress, a high-performance framework implementing three standard text game benchmarks that boosts simulation speed by a factor of 1,000, achieving more than one million steps per second on standard desktops. Our benchmarks show improved performance over current standards, offering a 400-fold speedup in Python and an 18 million-fold speedup when using the ctypes library. Text-based simulations are essential for training and evaluating advanced AI agents tasked with navigating their way home, performing household chores, or executing other real-world activities. While textWorld offers a simple platform for creating arbitrary text games, it is now 50 times slower than our implementation. We utilize textWorld as the foundation for TextWorldExpress, a high-performance library enabling users to design and simulate a wide range of text-based games. TextWorldExpress achieves this through three key advancements over textWorld: (1) it supports a diverse array of popular text game benchmarks, (2) it incorporates common toys and experiments from recent literature, and (3) it delivers ultra-high simulation speeds. a potent class of deep neural networks extensively utilized for sequence modeling. However, their substantial model size hinders deployment on resource-constrained edge devices, prompting the need to optimize their size and complexity for real-time inference. While knowledge distillation (KD) is a popular dimension-reduction technique, its application to LSTM networks is complex due to the difficulty in aligning non-linear hidden states between large student networks and simple linear output-based teacher networks. This paper introduces an efficient two-stage approach to compact LSTM networks: initially, we convert the LSTM into an equivalent feedforward structure using its unrolled architecture, followed by standard KD; subsequently, an auxiliary dimension is integrated via additional loss functions, leveraging the LSTM's long-term memory capability for more effective knowledge transfer. This two-stage method was inspired by recent findings indicating that integrating long-term memory is more crucial for successful KD than structural similarity. Our proposed method, termed ReMem (short for Reunrolled with Long-term Memory), achieves compact network results that outperform both current two-stage methods and traditional single-stage approaches on several real-world datasets. Source code is available at https://github.com/yuanying0207/Compact-LSTMs. Yuanying Ying and Jie Fu contributed equally to this work. Yuanying Ying is now with the University of Alberta, Canada; Jie Fu is with Amazon Web Services, USA.

We introduce a related yet distinct proposal: the conjecture should instead apply to particles possessing non-negative self-binding energy. This perspective is especially significant in anti-de Sitter (AdS) space, as it admits a straightforward conformal field theory (CFT) dual. Specifically, if $\Delta(q)$ represents the scaling dimension of the lowest-dimension operator carrying charge $q$ under a global $U(1)$ symmetry, then $\Delta(q)$ must be a convex function of $q$. Unlike formulations relying on holographic dual forces or spacetime locality, this approach allows us to boldly conjecture that charge spectrum convexity applies to any unitary CFT, extending beyond those with weakly coupled and weakly curved gravitational duals. We term this the Charge Convexity Conjecture and note its generalization to larger global symmetry groups. Testing this via perturbation theory, $1/N$ expansions, and semi-classical methods in examples where anomalous dimensions are calculable confirms the conjecture in all cases examined. However, the underlying CFT reason for this validity remains unclear. Furthermore, by leveraging the connection to entanglement entropy, we derive an intriguing implication: the F-theorem in 2+1 dimensions also relies on convexity. Finally, we link this charge convexity to a fundamental convexity property of thermal entropy and argue that such properties should underpin a conjecture for general quantum field theories (QFTs) regarding the subadditivity of von Neumann entropy. This study presents a mixed-integer linear programming model designed to identify the most capital-efficient power generation and transmission expansion strategies, incorporating a stochastic weather model for short- and medium-term operation planning. By integrating these two planning horizons, the model ensures feasibility across all historical weather patterns and future years. Planning for varying weather conditions enables a more realistic and risk-informed media expansion model, as it avoids relying on representive but potentially uncharacteristic typical meteorological years. Furthermore, accounting for increasing weather variability and extreme events through expanded meteorological probability distributions is now feasible with this approach. The model was developed using the Python-based open-source energy optimization tool PyPSA. To handle the resulting high-dimensional optimization problem efficiently, we utilized the parallelized, block-angular Deltat method, enhancing computational speed through a specialized two-phase algorithm. In this two-phase process, a bi-level algorithm first identifies linking variables separating different planning periods, after which the optimization proceeds in two stages: first solving for planning periods and subsequently for hours within a typical meteorological year. Plots and tables illustrating results from a planning domain spanning from power plants to distribution networks demonstrate that considering weather variability and extremes significantly alters expansion plans compared to using typical meteorological years. These findings underscore the necessity of advanced modeling for both short- and long-term optimization in the transition toward decentralized power production and consumption. The PyPSA software, together with the described two-phase algorithm, facilitates the adaptation of the model to other regions and planning domains. Since the model also accommodates other sources of uncertainty such as technology costs and demand, it serves as a robust foundation for researching the joint optimization of shorter planning horizons in conjunction with various uncertain factors.

spectroscopy to track the seasonal development and decay of large, warm vortices located poleward of approximately $75^\circ$ latitude in the stratosphere. These vortices initiate formation just south of the summer pole with sizes ranging from $35,000$ to $50,000$ km in diameter. Once they reach the solstice pole, they transform into "super-rotating" structures that expand to fill the entire polar cap, exhibiting characteristics similar to planetary-scale Rossby waves observed on Earth and Mars. While the poleward flow of this summer hemisphere is driven by radiative cooling, the equatorward flow relies on radiatively induced horizontal temperature gradients and the non-conservative nature of recirculating heat flux. This dynamical behavior, which includes tropical stratospheric sudden warming-like events, offers a complex precursor to the winter pole's thermal inversion and eventual polar cap vortex creation. This process significantly influences the long-term deposition and sequestration of photochemically generated species, such as hydrocarbon aerosols, in the winter atmosphere through the vortices' expansion and contraction, as well as in the equatorial region via the vortex's equatorward edge. These findings are based on thermal infrared observations from Cassini's final years and upstream solar wind data from ACE and Wind. During the 2017-2018 period, the Sun entered conjunction with Earth, limiting real-time communication and delaying the assessment of how the Recurrent Shocks Driven by the Solar Wind (RDS) influence the thermosphere during this event. Consequently, this study employs ground-based observations of ion outflows from the Cassini era, along with INCA and WIND in-situ data from prior years, to revisit the characteristics of RDS and their impact on ion outflows during the Janssen RDS in 2017. By applying these revised estimates to previous results on Venus ion outflows derived from RDS, a correlation is sought across different time scales. On one hand, the correlation between RDS intensity and the daily variable component of solar wind-dependent outflows (previously identified using INCA) is examined over the Conjunction Event. On the other hand, outflows on an orbital scale, which were found to be decoupled from solar wind parameters during the Janssen RDS, are analyzed after the event. This decoupling is attributed to a Large Scale Oblate Magnetic Field (LSOM) generated by the persistent RDS.

We demonstrate that solutions possessing negative energy exhibit finite-time blow-up. Additionally, under the assumption that the nonlinearity is energy-subcritical and given further symmetry constraints, we establish blow-up governed by the same optimal ground-state criterion found in Holmer and Roudenko's work on $\R^{d}$. The traditional Glassey proof, which relies on the concavity of variance, is inapplicable in the exterior of an obstacle due to boundary terms arising from the Dirichlet condition. To address this, our primary approach involves modifying the variance action model to eliminate these boundary terms, thereby extending the concavity argument to this setting. Furthermore, we introduce a reflection technique to transfer the spatial dimensionality restriction from $\R^{d}$ to $\SO(d)$. Our findings are also significant for the initial-value problem associated with the Schrödinger equation in the same external domain. In the process of proving finite-time blow-up, we gather essential properties of the ground-state energy for the corresponding elliptic problem with a negative well depth in the exterior of an obstacle, utilizing reflection methods and classical phase-plane analysis. The special case where the obstacle is a sphere was previously resolved by Hausler and Kowalczyk.

While scattering techniques offer valuable complementary data, they are constrained to electron-based probes, limiting their applicability. Central to spectroscopy is the transition dipole moment, a quantity that dictates how molecules absorb and emit light, reflecting changes in electron density and molecular geometry. Although time-dependent density functional theory (TD-DFT) is a standard computational tool for modeling transition dipole moments, it struggles with certain molecular systems and cannot fully represent long-range charge transfer excitations. Consequently, TD-DFT often yields inaccurate results when evaluated against experiment. In this study, we present calculations of transition dipole moments using two opposing many-body perturbation theory (MBPT) approaches: the random phase approximation (RPA) and GW-RPA. We further contrast these findings with RPA outcomes derived from both TD-DFT and the Green's Function-Self Consistent Field (GF-SCF) methods. GF-SCF serves as a cutting-edge computational technique that provides a non-perturbative description of molecular transitions, overcoming limitations inherent in both TD-DFT and MBPT frameworks. Collectively, these findings establish GF-SCF as a robust method for computing transition dipole moments across various molecular and crystalline systems. GF-SCF achieves this by solving the Green's Function exactly, incorporating strong correlation effects and avoiding the double counting of electron-electron interactions often found in competing methodologies. Ultimately, this research demonstrates that GF-SCF accurately captures both low and high-lying electronic excitations, making it a potent tool for probing molecular and crystal systems across the ultraviolet, visible, and infrared spectra. By precisely calculating transition dipole moments, GF-SCF enhances our understanding of light absorption and scattering processes, which are essential for diverse applications in solar energy, water splitting, organic light-emitting diodes, and Raman scattering. Although GF-SCF requires significantly more computational time than TD-DFT—potentially requiring supercomputing resources for larger systems—it produces more exacting and reliable results. Thus, GF-SCF represents a significant advancement over current computational methods for analyzing light-matter interactions. This research was conducted using the recently released VAMP GF-SCF code.

Although Bayes factors provide a direct approach to hypothesis evaluation, they are notably sensitive to specific data characteristics and model assumptions. Furthermore, their practical implementation remains uncertain regarding its robustness to computational details. This study examines these issues within the context of cognitive science applications. We clarify the statistical foundations of Bayes factors for Bayesian inference and emphasize the necessity of utility functions for making principled decisions. Additionally, we investigate the behavior of Bayes factors under various conditions, including errors in estimation. Notably, we demonstrate that Bayes factors can exhibit extreme values, ranging from intensely positive to strongly negative. In terms of estimation, we compare methods for computing approximate Bayes factors and their respective uncertainties. Our analysis reveals that while some approximate estimators are unbiased, others possess extreme variance; conversely, certain estimators with high variance may remain useful for estimating hypotheses that are not extremely close. We also assess the robustness of these estimators to numerical integration parameters. Finally, we evaluate the performance of these approaches using simulated data across several standard scenarios in cognitive science. Throughout this process, we discuss how these findings can aid in selecting hypotheses. All code is available on GitHub.

Recent studies have productively investigated predicting discourse markers between sentence pairs to derive accurate sentence representations beneficial for various classification tasks. This paper adopts a different approach: we utilize a model trained to predict discourse markers between sentence pairs to infer plausible markers for pairs with known semantic relations (sourced from existing classification datasets). Although handcrafted mappings have been suggested between markers and discourse relations for limited sets of markers and categories, hundreds of discourse markers express a diverse range of relations, and there is no agreed-upon taxonomy of relations among competing theories (which are predominantly constructed top-down). The resulting dataset, called DiscSense, is publicly accessible. Our analysis of DiscSense reinforces the notion that markers can express multiple relations and reveals that the majority of discourse relation types can be accounted for by a relatively small number of markers. By applying the Burer-Monteiro factorization within a specific Riemannian quotient geometry defined on a search space equipped with a Euclidean metric, we analyze the global landscape of the resulting factorized objective. Assuming the original objective function $f$ adheres to standard restricted strong convexity and smoothness conditions, we demonstrate that the entire search space partitions into three distinct regions: (R1) a neighborhood around the target parameter where the objective is geodesically strongly convex and smooth; (R2) areas surrounding all strict saddle points; and (R3) remaining regions characterized by large gradients. To our knowledge, this constitutes the first global landscape analysis of the Burer-Monteiro factorized objective under this specific Riemannian quotient geometry. These findings offer a complete geometric rationale for the enhanced performance of vanilla gradient descent in this context. Furthermore, under a weaker restricted strict convexity assumption, we establish that geodesic convexity holds in a neighborhood of local minimizers. Our proofs rely on a detailed landscape analysis of a matrix factorization problem with a least squares objective, serving as a pivotal intermediate step. Additionally, our conclusions rest on a standalone result identifying that the geodesic ball centered at $Y$ with a radius equal to one-third of $Y$'s least singular value forms a geodesically convex set under the Riemannian quotient geometry. These results extend to a general matrix factorization objective under the same restricted strong convexity and smoothness assumptions, providing a restricted strongly convex and smooth neighborhood around local minimizers for its factorized objective. Numerical experiments underscore the significance of restricting the search space to ensure geodesic convexity near the solution. Finally, we outline potential extensions to other constrained objectives and alternative search spaces.

now integral to many safety-critical computer vision tasks, such as automated driving and human-robot interaction. To ensure reliability in real-world deployments, these systems must remain robust against hardware soft errors that corrupt platform memory. Building on the proven effectiveness of activation clipping, this study constructs a preliminary safety case for classifier CNNs by showing that range supervision acts as a highly dependable fault detector and mitigator for relevant bit flips, specifically within an eight-exponent floating-point format. Additionally, we investigate novel, non-uniform range restriction techniques that successfully reduce the likelihood of silent data corruptions and uncorrectable errors. As a practical, safety-critical end-to-end demonstration, we apply our method to a vehicle classification task using ResNet-50 and the MIOVision traffic camera dataset. The quantitative results presented here can serve as a foundation for developing further, potentially more sophisticated, safety arguments for CNNs. Safety concerns are increasingly relevant to the fields of software-defined and machine learning-based systems, particularly regarding their adoption in safety-critical applications. These concerns extend beyond traditional issues like specification errors and attacks; hardware soft errors are a primary source of random, hard-to-detect, and mitigate failures in safety-critical real-time systems. Although the error rates of modern commercial hardware are generally low, the complexity of systems like software-defined and neural networks means that even infrequent, uncorrectable soft errors can trigger system crashes or unsafe behaviors. Consequently, soft errors represent a significant, often overlooked hazard in safety-critical contexts. This paper demonstrates range restriction's efficacy as a dependable safety mechanism against bit flips and other random hardware soft errors for classifier CNNs. Our approach involves straightforward, conservative, and potentially dynamic activation clipping strategies. We provide a quantitative safety argument by connecting the error characteristics of a specific floating-point memory access format with the decision boundaries of a CNN classifier. To make this argument practical, we apply the argument to a real-world vehicle classifier (an eight-exponent floating-point format) and a popular CNN architecture (ResNet-50) trained on a vehicle classification dataset (MIOVision). Our findings reveal a high dependence of bit flips on activation magnitude and that our clipping methods can both detect and correct these bit flips. Overall, this work underscores the necessity of considering hardware soft errors when developing safety cases for CNNs and demonstrates that simple, transparent, and potentially adaptive activation range restriction methods can form the basis of such safety cases. Safety-related topics are currently under active research and discussion in the domains of machine learning and real-time systems.

**1 Introduction**

Accessing knowledge in new languages is essential for advancing Natural Language Processing (NLP). This need is particularly acute in low-resource linguistics, where a lack of annotated data hinders the adoption of modern NLP technologies. Although multilingual Neural Machine Translation (NMT) is a primary application for such systems, it is not the only one; other cross-lingual tasks include language identification, document translation, and even code development. Currently, researchers often struggle to adapt monolingual models and datasets to additional languages because standard common embedding spaces are difficult to construct. Existing techniques for finding equivalent words across languages focus on neural methods that rely on large parallel corpora—resources that are frequently unavailable—and these methods lack interpretability. There is a clear need for a straightforward method to learn a common semantic space using resources available in every language.

To better understand the quantum thermodynamics of many-body systems, we investigate whether the QNEC constrains irreversible entropy production during entanglement swapping of two spatial halves in a thermal state of one or two harmonic oscillators. For a single oscillator, we show that while the standard second law of thermodynamics is not strictly obeyed for small temperatures or large distances between the oscillators, the QNEC remains valid. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the non-violation of the QNEC enables the formulation of a second-order correction to the first law of thermodynamics, effectively extending the second law. In the case of two coupled oscillators, we observe violations of the QNEC that result in exceptions to the second law of thermodynamics. These violations arise from the non-uniformity of the quantum state and can be understood by comparing the entanglement production rate with the non-equilibrium fluctuations of the first and second laws of thermodynamics. Our results indicate that two small systems strongly coupled to a thermal bath can exhibit behavior contradicting the second law, as first proposed by Maxwell's demon. However, this does not imply the absence of a generalized second law, since the QNEC lower bound on the first and second law non-equilibrium contributions to the second small system's irreversible entropy production exceeds the entropy decrease of the thermal bath. To our knowledge, this study is the first to utilize the QNEC to extend the second law of thermodynamics and the inaugural to violate it. This work contributes to the field of quantum gravity/quantum information duality by applying the QNEC to a simple model beyond the conformal field theory approximation. To achieve this, our calculations employ a numerical approach utilizing the path integral formulation of the von Neumann entropy through the thermo field dynamics technique. Our findings suggest that the violation of the QNEC is directly linked to the non-equilibrium violation of the second law of thermodynamics, whereas the second small system's irreversible entropy production accounts for the decrease in the thermal bath's entropy, ensuring the validity of the generalized second law of thermodynamics. These conclusions align with recent studies on the connection between the QNEC and the second law of thermodynamics. Ultimately, the violation of the QNEC can be viewed as a mechanism allowing for the non-trivial fulfillment of the second law of thermodynamics.

For unitary evolution driven by a time-independent Hamiltonian, we establish a necessary and sufficient condition involving two asymmetry monotones that ensures any state of a two-level system or a separable state of $N$ two-level systems can evolve unitarily into a distinguishable state with a fixed minimal error probability $\delta \in [0,1/2]$. This condition facilitates ordering qubit states by their distinguishability time and determines the optimal release time for driven two-level systems, such as those found in the Landau-Zener scenario. Regarding non-unitary dynamics, we evaluate three lower bounds for the distinguishability time, introducing a novel bound defined by the asymmetry of the uniformly time-twirled initial system-plus-environment state in the Stinespring representation. We illustrate these Distinguishability Time bounds across several models, including the optimal cloning of a two-level system, the decoherence of a qubit due to environmental coupling, and the Landau-Zener model. Notably, our calculations for the Landau-Zerem show that the distinguishability time for qubits is significantly shorter when quantum operations are non-unitary compared to their unitary counterparts. We further generalize these results to apply to any operation feasible via a quantum channel. This work extends the concept of thermodynamic cost for state discrimination to encompass all feasible quantum operations. Notably, we introduce a time-asymmetry cost for state discrimination, which, unlike its thermodynamic equivalent, can be negative, occurring when a initially indistinguishable state can be made distinguishable through quantum evolution. This negative cost signifies a benefit in the efficiency of quantum communication and computation. The processes that formed and evolved Venus's atmosphere to its current surface conditions remain subjects of intense debate, encompassing questions that span multiple disciplines. We investigate these interconnected mechanisms, beginning with volatile sources and sinks related to accretion, differentiation, and late heavy bombardment. Subsequent sections address geodynamical and geological volatile cycles, followed by surface-atmosphere cycles, and conclude with shallow geological and geothermal cycles. Finally, these cycles are integrated into simple models to explore their collective impact on Venus's history and to assess the likelihood of current cycles sustaining trace gases detected by the *Akatsuki* mission. While Venus lacks plate tectonics, making the geodynamical water cycle distinct from Earth's, the absence of a significant magnetic field renders the atmospheric water cycle between the planet and atmosphere crucial. The geodynamical water cycle is now better understood following the identification of surface impacts that expose putative water reservoirs. In contrast, constraints on the geochemical and geothermal water cycles remain largely unbounded, as the necessary data and methodologies are predominantly applicable to Earth or moons possessing subsurface oceans. Without seismological or geodetic observations to locate active volcanism or impact sites, and lacking in-situ measurements of gas isotopes, mineralogies, or the site and magnitude of water cycles, evaluating the presence and cycling of volatiles on Venus remains highly speculative. Although Akatsuki has detected trace gases and anomalies indicating potentially active volcanic or impact sites, interpreting these findings requires an updated assessment of Venus's activity. This report outlines the various volatile cycles on Venus and their effects on the atmosphere's composition and cloud chemistry, aiming to identify the most probable locations and sources of the trace gases observed by Akatsuki.

The Hawkes process, introduced by A.G. Hawkes in \[15, 16\], is a self-exciting point process where the likelihood of additional events is driven by past occurrences. SN~2020jfo emerged roughly 1.6~years after the merger of GW190814, a event featuring a gravitational-wave signal that extended to higher frequencies than any other detected by LIGO/Virgo. While the spectral features and early-evolution traits of SN~2020jfo initially suggested it originated from the disruption of a donor star in a remnant black hole system following GW190814, the swift influx of angular momentum would have likely spun up the new black hole beyond its massaccrition limit. However, the swift arrival of SN~2020jfo aligns with the tidal disruption of a main-sequence star by the GW190814 remnant. We demonstrate that the views and energy distribution of SN~2020jfo match those expected from the fastest disruptions observed to date. Furthermore, the fact that the GW190814 remnant retained enough mass to produce a visible supernova implies that the object is not a neutron star, but rather the lightest possible black hole. Together, these findings suggest that the sub-3~M$\odot$ gap between the neutron star and black hole mass spectra is not continuous. This conclusion reinforces the concept of a massaccrition boundary above the maximum neutron star mass and indicates that the lower boundary of the black hole mass spectrum is dictated by the properties of the most compact donors feasible for tidal disruption. Ultimately, SN~2020jfo offers the first direct view of the bottom of the black hole mass spectrum and demonstrates that objects in this mass range can retain significant donor remnants to produce visible fast transients. The spin of the GW190814 remnant, derived from the arrival time of SN~2020jfo, may help clarify the formation channels of these enigmatic mid-mass gravitational wave sources. SN~2020jfo can be identified with previously reported candidates associated with GW190814, including Swift~J190114-3640, XRT~J190114.0-364030, and i~20200702a.
