Designed with quasi-static evolutionary applications in mind, our method utilizes a custom-developed Lagrangian formulation. Unlike the standard Eulerian approach, this formulation solves force balance equations to determine the positions of fluid elements mapped to grid points. Distinct from prior literature, we do not rely on the first integral of the Euler equation, which typically lacks a general analytic solution. Instead of prescribing the spatial distribution of angular velocity or angular momentum as previous methods do, we assign specific mass, angular momentum, and entropy to each fluid element; the angular velocity and momentum distributions are subsequently derived once the positions of all elements are established. We discretize the time-independent Euler and Einstein equations using the finite-element method, resulting in a large system of nonlinear algebraic equations that we solve via our new multi-dimensional root-finding algorithm, the W4 method. To validate this formulation, we have constructed both barotropic and baroclinic rotational configurations and solved three evolutionary sequences that simulate cooling, mass loss, and mass accretion as simplified toy models. Furthermore, we present the open-source relstarfem software, which features significant algorithmic and code structure improvements over its predecessor relstarv2. Relstarfem offers several advantages for future research, including a more efficient algorithm that requires fewer computation nodes and a refined code architecture that facilitates the integration of new physical components and evolutionary operators. Comparisons with related Lagrangian and Eulerian codes demonstrate that our method effectively computes configuration properties, such as mass, angular momentum, and radius, with high precision. Additionally, the code accurately renders complex star shapes, including ellipsoidal, egg-like, and bean-shaped structures. While the final angular masses of our computed barotropic configurations align closely with those from other methods, they exhibit superior numerical stability. Additionally, the baroclinic configurations generated by relstarfem achieve high precision in angular momentum distribution profiles and density contours when directly compared to recent three-dimensional results. Although relstarfem shares the same foundational advantages over traditional Eulerian codes—namely higher numerical stability and precision, and the absence of advection errors—the final solutions were obtained with coarser meshing. We anticipate that algorithmic and code enhancements will soon enable this efficient solver to calculate time-evolution models for various astrophysical scenarios, such as neutron star binaries. Relstarfem represents a significant advancement over relstarv2, offering a more robust and scalable computational platform for astrophysical applications.

Document layout analysis is essential for enabling computers to process unstructured texts found in industry documents, such as web forms, medical reports, and invoices. Specifically, extracting all entities from documents is a fundamental step for many downstream tasks. However, significant challenges remain in developing effective layouts extraction methods for real-world documents. This paper addresses the task of extracting all key entities from invoices. We develop a end-to-end approach to recognize all entity instances, rather than just the head and tail entities commonly targeted in prior work. This approach is built around three core components: (1) a header embedding module that generates robust embeddings for each company-specific tag to facilitate effective entity extraction across diverse invoices; (2a) a component that leverages the structured nature of invoices and the learned header embeddings to directly locate all entity positions within document bodies; and (2b) a component that utilizes a bi-encoder cross attention model to resolve conflicts when entities appear multiple times, ensuring all unique instances are captured; and (3) an all-into-few component that iteratively refines the document representation by treating the ground truth of already extracted entities as intermediate "few" labels to support accurate extraction of remaining entities. Experimental results on two real-world invoice datasets show that our method significantly surpasses state-of-the-art techniques for all-into-few extraction, and we also present findings on head-and-tail extraction. Additionally, we offer a open-source framework allowing researchers to apply various extraction techniques on different document kinds using our in-house invoice dataset. For events involving neutron stars, the concurrent detection of gravitational and electromagnetic radiation offers significant potential to deepen our understanding of these phenomena and investigate the equation of state of dense matter. Furthermore, we project the sensitivity of third-generation instruments to NSBH mergers and the corresponding redshift range for the observable events. This study examines a rotationally invariant variant of L1-PCA theoretically and connects it to $\ell_1$-SVD and $\ell_1$-canonical correlations. A key finding of our work is the non-asymptotic analysis of $\ell_1$-PCA in high dimensions, specifically regarding principal component estimation in linear dimensional reduction tasks with outliers. Additionally, we demonstrate through simulations that our non-asymptotic bounds are reasonably tight. Our main contributions include a comprehensive theoretical analysis and original empirical results presented in this paper's appendix, which offer a detailed numerical evaluation of various dimensional reduction methods with outliers, illustrating the practical efficacy of the proposed approach. In this study, we introduce a Mach-Zehnder atomic interferometry setup designed to measure extremely weak local magnetic fields expelled by a superconductor—acting as a "testing magnet"—via the Meissner effect. The resulting magnetic field gradient near the superconductor generates a centripetal acceleration on the atoms within the interferometer, enabling detection through atomic interference patterns. Building on the fact that gravitational acceleration of atoms has been measured with a precision of $10^{-12}$ g, the sensitivity of this method for detecting the expelled local field could potentially achieve $10^{-14}$ T. Our proposed apparatus comprises three main sections: the expelled magnetic field region, the atomic interferometer, and the sample holder holding the superconductor. The design ensures that the expelled field is the sole varying acceleration gradient across the width of the expelled field exclusion region, while the supergravity gradient remains constant throughout the atomic cloud. Although this is a concept paper, it provides all necessary theoretical and experimental details to guide actual device construction. If built, this Mach-Zehnder atomic interferometer could offer the highest sensitivity for measuring the Meissner effect and the expelled local magnetic field. Furthermore, this setup may find broader applications, such as precisely quantifying the magnetic field gradient generated by anti-matter. rather than qubits for the variational quantum linear solver (VQLS) algorithm. VQLS was introduced to apply variational quantum algorithms to the important task of solving systems of linear equations. While the approach is sound, previous implementations have been limited to small-scale problems due to challenges in optimizing the variational ansatz. Although increasing ansatz depth offers the potential for improved performance, this comes at the cost of heightened susceptibility to noise. To address this, we propose using qudits instead of qubits to construct a VQLS ansatz. Our method yields a compact variational qudit ansatz that requires fewer parameters and possesses higher dimensionality. This strategy allows us to solve a selected linear system with a significantly reduced ansatz compared to the qudit-binary VQLS ansatz, which is capable of solving the same system. Furthermore, our approach can be applied to any linear system. Empirical results demonstrate that our method is both robust and efficient. We contend that the efficacy of using qudits for VQLS is evident, and this strategy represents a straightforward途径 to developing more advanced variants of the VQLS algorithm. This study utilizes QED particle-in-cell simulations that incorporate electron-positron spin and photon polarization to examine a standard laser-solid configuration where an ultraintense linearly polarized laser strikes a foil target featuring a micrometer-scale preplasma. Our results indicate that when laser intensity surpasses $10^{24}~\rm W/\rm cm^2$ and positron yield becomes significant, the produced positrons exhibit clear polarization. Specifically, these polarized positrons can achieve a polarization degree exceeding 20% and a charge greater than 3 nC, with a flux of 100% of the generated charge and an energy average above 5 MeV. The underlying mechanism involves positrons radiating polarized photons before accelerating and radiating further within the laser field, a process we term "radiative radiative polarization." This phenomenon represents a radiative effect distinct from radiative self-polarization, which has been documented in prior works. Furthermore, this radiative radiative polarization is most prominent at laser charges of gamma factors ranging from 3 to 7 and can be intensified by increasing the laser charge. Additionally, the degree of positron polarization can be further enhanced by optimizing target conditions, such as reducing preplasma thickness or employing sinusoidal laser waveforms. These capabilities offer significant potential for various applications, including precision tests of particle physics and antimatter properties, free-electron lasers, $\mu$-cathode positron sources, and scanning beams. We have also derived a semi-analytical formula to estimate the degree of positron polarization. This is the initial demonstration of positron polarization in dense laser-solid interactions and expands upon the understanding of radiative effects in this domain by introducing the concept of radiative radiative polarization, which can occur at laser charges of gamma factors between 2 and 10. Experimental verification is currently feasible. However, it is worth noting that if the preplasma charge exceeds approximately 6 times the elementary charge ($6\rm ~e$), the degree of positron polarization may diminish or vanish, a factor that must be considered during experimental design. This research paves the way for producing high-quality polarized positron beams through future laser-solid interactions.

Abramson and Parashar contend that a comparable divide exists between sophisticated computational technologies and increasingly demanding applications, necessitating a parallel field known as translational computer science. In this discipline, the intentional transition of research findings into large-scale practice becomes a primary research objective rather than a secondary consideration. Examining the evolution and deployment of grid computing from the mid-1990s through this lens reveals that a translational framework effectively elucidates both the technology's development and its impact. Specifically, the growth of grid computing infrastructure and the Globus Toolkit was facilitated by this translational methodology. Furthermore, the authors highlight key lessons derived from these experiences that can inform future translational computer science endeavors. Abstract translational computer science serves as a potent tool for identifying promising technological trajectories, such as the in-memory distributed systems explored in this paper. Additionally, the lessons learned in translational grid computing offer valuable insights for system architects developing systems like the Hadoop ecosystem. Abstract translational computer science functions as a robust lens for analyzing technological advancement, while a translational framework provides a concrete guide to building systems that deliver tangible benefits.

Systems with non-convex loss functions are now widely employed in applications ranging from knowledge discovery to intelligent transportation. Our approach utilizes a multi-table data model to represent loss landscape characteristics and loss landscape maps to visualize them. This system, which we have open-sourced as Translational DL, was validated through various experiments demonstrating significant advancements in training deep neural networks. (IShTAR) serves as a specialized facility at the Max-Planck Institute for Plasma Physics in Garching, Germany, designed to study the interaction between ICRF waves and plasma. A plasma source, measuring 0.15 meters in length and 0.10 meters in diameter, is positioned at the center of the IShTAR magnet system to generate the plasma. This source features a helical antenna on its side, enabling a source-cyclotron resonance that allows for efficient, low-pressure ion cyclotron heating. This mechanism significantly narrows the cyclotron resonance, concentrating power deposition within a specific magnetic field range corresponding to the ion mass. Consequently, this plasma source is particularly well-suited for creating high-density Xenon plasma for IShTAR applications. This paper presents the initial characterization of both the plasma source and the heating system, including local power deposition analysis, magnetic field mapping, and cyclotron resonance scanning. The results demonstrate the potential for varying cyclotron resonance positions along the magnetic field gradient by adjusting the driving frequency, alongside high-density production (up to $2.5 \times 10^{13} cm^{-3}$) and rapid particle confinement release using a virtual grid. Finally, these capabilities are linked to the proposed IShTAR experiment configuration. Keywords: ICRF heating, ion cyclotron resonance, plasma source, magnetic mirror, IShTAR, virtual grid, xenon.

Nucleus segmentation technology is commonly employed to automate these tasks; however, training robust segmentation models remains challenging due to issues like nucleus adhesion, stacking, and excessive background fusion. Although recent approaches based on point annotation have significantly enhanced model performance, they still require experienced pathologists to provide the necessary annotations. To leverage the benefits of point-annotation-based methods while reducing manual workload and improving the efficiency and accuracy of cancer diagnosis, an automatic nucleus detection algorithm is needed to efficiently locate nuclei and extract valuable information from pathological images. This paper introduces a W-shaped network for automatic nucleus detection. Unlike traditional U-Net-based methods that directly map pathology images to target masks, our approach decomposes the detection task into two sub-tasks: first mapping the original image to a binary mask, and then mapping that binary mask to a density mask. This task splitting significantly reduces complexity and enhances the network's overall performance. Experimental results on the BCDN dataset demonstrate that our method outperforms several state-of-the-art algorithms in terms of F-score, mean accuracy, and mean absolute error for nucleus counting, with statistical analyses confirming the efficacy of the proposed method. Source code is available at: https://github.com/zhengyuan2002/Wshaped-Network.

coupled to a scalar field featuring a two-parameter Higgs-like self-interaction is reformulated using a Chern-Simons form associated with the algebra $g^{+}\oplus g^{-}$. Depending on the sign of the self-interaction couplings, the components $g^{\pm}$ correspond to $so(2,2)$, $so(3,1)$, or $iso(2,1)$. The field equations are expressed via the field strength of non-flat composite gauge fields, allowing conserved charges to be derived from boundary terms in the action. These charges align with standard pure gravity Chern-Simons theory but utilize non-flat connections. Field regularity is ensured by requiring trivial holonomy of the connections along contractible cycles; this condition is naturally satisfied by scalar solitons. Consequently, the Hawking temperature and chemical potential for rotating hairy black holes can be recovered, and their entropy is calculated using the same formula applicable to pure Chern-Simons theory. Additionally, within the conformal (Jordan) frame, the theory represents General Relativity with a cosmological constant conformally coupled to a self-interacting scalar field, and its description via a Chern-Simons form for appropriately constructed composite gauge fields is also presented. Finally, the self-consistency of this approach is verified by ensuring that the theory's global symmetries correctly map to its conserved currents. This reformulation offers an alternative to the AdS/CFT holographic dictionary, potentially extending to higher dimensions and dimensions greater than three, and provides a straightforward method for computing black hole entropy in coupled scalar-field systems with arbitrary profiles.

Accurate mechanical property estimation requires solving an inverse problem, which depends on accurately measuring the spatial and temporal ultrasound signal shifts caused by tissue motion. While the Fourier transform improves transform-domain signal-to-noise ratios, it lacks the time-localization capabilities necessary for analyzing nonstationary signals. This insight motivates a broader generalization of pseudocode, termed *logical pseudocodes*, which parallels natural deduction proofs within computability logic \cite{Jap03,Jap08}. The fundamental advantage of forward reasoning over backward reasoning in logical pseudocodes, as noted in literature such as \cite{DBLP:books-elr/Rey97}, is the absence of the backtracking algorithm. within the dynamic streaming framework, where points from a discrete grid can be dynamically added or removed. Our primary contribution introduces a new online clustering approach that operates efficiently over grids, both in standard $k$-means cost terms and regarding the $k$-nearest neighbor cost metric. This algorithm achieves an $O(k\cdot \text{opt})$-approximation for standard $k$-means cost and a $\sqrt{k\cdot \text{opt}}$-approximation for the $k$-nearest neighbor cost, where $\text{opt}$ represents the optimal cost. The method is designed for float2int grids (grid points are multiples of a parameter $int \geq 1$); by selecting $int$ equal to the range of input floats, we obtain a deterministic online algorithm for real numbers that incurs only minimal extra space and update time overheads. Furthermore, the algorithm is highly space-efficient, requiring $O(k \log n \log n \log \log n)$ bits. In the specific case of power-of-2 grids, the algorithm achieves $O(\text{opt})$-approximation for standard $k$-means cost and $O(\sqrt{\text{opt}})$-approximation for the $k$-nearest neighbor cost with $O(k \log n)$ update time and $O(k \log n \log n)$ update amplitude. These results represent significant improvements upon the current state of the art for dynamic streaming $k$-means, particularly in update time, update amplitude, and space efficiency. The algorithm supports non-uniform distributions of points across the grid and remains effective even when the number of points per cell is low. Experimental evidence suggests that the actual update time is often substantially lower than the theoretical bound. Additionally, the framework generalizes to multi-key $k$-means and other similar cost functions. The implementation is publicly available at https://github.com/yairhuhn/StreamKMeans. The code was written in C++ and utilized the Massively Parallel Computation (MPC) library. Keywords: $k$-means, Dynamic Data Streams, MPC.

By segmenting the grid into superstates, such as "rooms," the method establishes a dual-resolution decision-making system comprising local PEGs at the granular state level and an aggregated PEG at the superstate level. Due to their reduced state space size, both the local and aggregated games can be efficiently solved to reach a Nash equilibrium. To bridge these two levels of decision-making, the Nash values derived from the local PEGs serve as rewards for the aggregated game. Numerical simulations demonstrate that this hierarchical approach substantially lowers computational costs while preserving performance comparable to flat Nash policies during competition. Furthermore, during deployment, the agent prioritates the execution of the Nash policy within its local room; if evasion is compromised, it escapes to a new room and resumes the local Nash policy. Numerical results indicate that this strategy maintains the benefits of Nash policies—such as significantly extended survival times in a 1000-state grid during a 1D PEG, or survival times 6.34 times longer in a 50x50 "maze" grid. Additionally, in an evolutionary setting where agents learn to solve these mazes, the majority successfully navigate and maintain survival times near those observed in the non-evolutionary maze scenario. In all cases, the computational complexity remains low and scales appropriately with grid dimensions. The codebase for this hierarchical PEG model is publicly accessible at https://github.com/AryaTavani/Hierarchical-PEGs. This paper presents an analysis of 34 years of Arecibo data regarding PSR B1133+16, yielding high-quality dynamic spectra and their corresponding scintillation arcs generated by screens along the line of sight. We identified six distinct screens responsible for these long-lasting arcs. Assuming the screens remained relatively stable over this period, we modeled their time-averaged locations using simple physics-based assumptions. By comparing these modeled positions with those derived from data, we determined that our approach is generally accurate, yet it underestimates the distance to the closest screen by approximately 1.4 kpc. Furthermore, we observed that signals from this nearest screen exhibit the strongest time variability. These findings indicate that our simple model fails to capture the dynamic nature of this screen and suggest the need for a more sophisticated modeling approach, especially given the cluster of screens along this particular line of sight. Ultimately, our model likely overlooks intermediate structures between the stars and the solar system that form part of the local interstellar medium. The six identified lines of sight hosting multiple screens offer an excellent opportunity to gain insights into the structure and properties of the local interstellar medium.

Audio enhancement is critical for improving speech recognition in real-world conditions and has been the subject of extensive research. This study presents a new approach to single-talker audio enhancement that integrates domain adaptation with performance evaluation across both visible and invisible test domains. First, we develop a domain-adapted single-talker enhancement framework based on the Wavenet architecture. To optimize results in unseen domains, a small number of target-domain audio pairs are employed to fine-tune the model after initial training on source-domain data. Second, we propose a evaluation method based on audio waveform drawings (AWD), which applies an adversarial domain discriminator to Wavenet-generated signals from both visible and invisible domains to assess the improvement in perceptual quality following domain adaptation. Quantitative and qualitative analyses indicate that this proposed method and the corresponding evaluation strategy are effective. The code is open-source at https://github.com/YifeiWan/Domain-Adapted-Audio-Enhancement. Index Terms—audio enhancement, domain adaptation, waveform generation, quasi-periodic signals, wavelet transform.

By leveraging Berman's extension of THH to bicategories, we establish an equivalence between functors originating from the THH of a bicategory and shadows defined on that same bicategory. This result enables a novel, conceptual demonstration of the Morita invariance of shadows. Furthermore, our framework generalizes THH and its topological extensions to monoidal categories, thereby offering fresh perspectives on existing constructions within a broader context. Finally, we apply these methods to create a new, rigorous, and explicit account of THH for monoidal categories. This explicit model serves as a crucial ingredient in a forthcoming proof of the Morita invariance of $E_n$-algebras via the fully faithfulness of THH for such algebras. Along the way, we also establish an equivalence between maps between CHH (Craik-Hyland homology) and THH for monoidal categories, extending a previous result by Hyland. Alongside an natural transformation linking CHH and THH, this equivalence provides a novel, explicit, and rigorous account of CHH for monoidal categories. Additionally, we present an explicit model for THH involving non-abelian complexes and prove its equivalence to the standard construction by an abstract criterion. An important feature of this model is its compatibility with the bar construction for non-abelian complexes, which facilitates the proof of the equivalence with the traditional model. Finally, we demonstrate the compatibility of our explicit model with base change, a property that was open regarding the standard model. This compatibility yields an explicit version of the five lemma for THH over monoidal categories and establishes the model's utility in computing THH for specific examples, such as Galtmac's THH of groupoids with coefficients.

### I. Introduction

Understanding the connection between visible sound sources and the audio tracks in videos is both a captivating theoretical question and a practical challenge with broad real-world applications. This capability has significant potential across diverse fields, including marketing, law enforcement, journalism, and healthcare. For instance, identifying the visible source of human speech helps separate audio streams in crowded environments where individuals are only partially visible. Similarly, locating visible sound sources aids in filtering misleading online news by verifying whether alleged events (e.g., factory explosions) are actually visible in the footage. Although recent efforts have advanced visible sound source localization (VSSL), many existing approaches rely on video segments annotated with bounding boxes around the object emitting sound. However, curating such labeled video-clips is labor-intensive and computationally expensive, creating a barrier to widespread application. Consequently, there is a clear need for efficient algorithms that can leverage "easy" video data (where annotations are absent) to learn robust VSSL representations. In this paper, we address the task of locating visible sound sources using only video clips and sound emissions, where the only annotation is a short segment indicating the time when the object is visible.

To address this, recent models have been developed to function in non-Euclidean spaces, particularly hyperbolic geometry. Although hyperbolic GCNs demonstrate promising results, current hyperbolic graph operations fail to strictly adhere to hyperbolic geometry, potentially limiting the space's utility and degrading model performance. This paper introduces a novel hyperbolic GCN, the Lorentzian graph convolutional network (LGCN), which ensures that learned node features rigorously conform to hyperbolic geometry. Specifically, we reconstruct key hyperbolic graph operations, such as feature transformation and non-linear activation, using their Lorentzian counterparts. Additionally, we propose an efficient neighborhood aggregation method grounded in Lorentzian distance centroids. We further demonstrate the equivalence of these proposed operations across different types of hyperbolic geometry, providing fundamental proof of their correctness. Experiments across six datasets reveal that LGCN outperforms state-of-the-art methods and exhibits lower distortion when learning node features compared to existing hyperbolic GCNs. Furthermore, we observe that the intrinsic dimension of Möbius geometry is at least twice that of Lorentzian geometry, suggesting that LGCN may require fewer computational resources than other hyperbolic GCNs. The source code is available at https://github.com/zhengruicai/LGCN.

All findings in the paper are experimental; the presented system models the interaction between an interior acoustic field and an adjacent plate structure, a configuration that is ubiquitous in engineering applications where understanding source characteristics from boundary measurements is crucial. Although the geometric derivation of the Weibull distribution is well-established, numerous attempts have been made to derive it combinatorially. This paper presents another such derivation and uses it to provide a combinatorial proof of the identity known as the generalized Abel identity. We prove that the $n$-th term of a sequence $a_n(x)$, defined recursively by $a_n(x) = x a_{n-1}(x) + (n+1)a_{n-2}(x+1)$ with initial conditions $a_0(x) = 1$ and $a_1(x) = a_1(0) = x$, is given by the formula:
$$a_n(x) = \sum_{k=0}^n \binom{n}{k} x^{k+1} a_{n-k-1}(x+1).$$
This result generalizes the generalized Abel identity:
$$\sum_{k=0}^n \binom{n}{k} a_k(x) a_{n-k}(y) = a_{n+1}(x+y).$$
Additionally, we establish a combinatorial interpretation for the sequence $a_n(x)$ and provide a similar interpretation for the expression on the right-hand side of the generalized Abel identity. Upon implementing this condition via the standard Faddeev-Popov procedure, the resulting gauge-fixed action retains a dependence on a single gauge parameter. This indicates that the harmonic gauge represents a family of conditions rather than a unique one. This perspective provides a physical justification for covariant harmonic gauges, which arise when a mass term is introduced for the gravitational perturbation. Specifically, selecting a particular harmonic gauge yields a theory of linearized massive gravity with the expected five degrees of freedom, successfully avoiding the vDVZ discontinuity that plagues the standard Fierz-Pauli theory. Furthermore, we demonstrate that a Lee-Wick type avoidance of this discontinuity emerges when the mass term takes a negative value. This scenario corresponds to a free theory describing a symmetric tensor with five degree of freedom poles at zero and negative mass scales, alongside a spin-zero pole at the negative mass scale; this result aligns with previous findings in four dimensions. We also offer interpretations of these poles in terms of forward and backward in time propagation. Additionally, we present the theory in the St\"uckelberg formalism and derive its master action. Beyond its intrinsic significance, this free theory serves as the linear approximation for pure massive gravity, a fact we utilize to derive the master action for that system. Beyond its relevance to massive gravity, the harmonic gauge with a negative mass parameter finds applications in inflationary cosmology involving scalar-tensor-vector gravity and massive gravity with a Galileon self-interaction term. An overview of subsequent developments regarding these topics is included.

This concise report utilizes the frameworks of statistical mechanics and thermodynamics to elucidate various facets of negative temperature within a two-level system, providing both mathematical and graphical explanations. By extending the simplest "missing partner" type-I seesaw with the minimal dark sector, we establish a physical mechanism for neutrino oscillation lengths: the atmospheric mass scale originates from tree-level seesaw dynamics, whereas the solar scale emerges radiatively through mediation by the dark sector. We pinpoint parameter regions that satisfy theoretical constraints, align with dark matter relic density, and are viable under direct detection limits. Employing two-loop renormalization group equations, we investigate vacuum stability and the consistency of the fundamental dark parity symmetry, while also deriving a lower bound for the neutrinoless double beta decay amplitude. Finally, we outline distinctive signatures for future LHC runs and delineate the impact of this model on neutrinoless double beta decay and neutrino oscillation probability asymmetries. The described mechanism offers a general approach to generating neutrino mass and explains the observed hierarchy among mass scales, potentially accounting for the unusually non-degenerate first mass eigenstate. This framework requires at least two heavy right-handed neutrinos with masses around 10 TeV to reproduce the atmospheric mass scale via tree-level seesaw dynamics. Concurrently, the remaining light right-handed neutrinos (below the dark sector's symmetry breaking scale) and the dark sector itself produce the solar mass scale via radiative seesaw dynamics, simultaneously explaining dark matter and adhering to neutrino oscillation data. Consequently, this model can be tested at the LHC via lepton-number-violating signatures from right-handed neutrinos and by refining predictions for neutrinoless double beta decay and neutrino oscillation probability asymmetries. This constitutes a testable, phenomenologically rich, and aesthetically pleasing alternative to the conventional "missing partner" type-I seesaw for establishing the mass hierarchy. Furthermore, unlike other models, it naturally accounts for the smallness of the neutrino mass without invoking the hierarchy problem, and it generates the sub-dominant mass eigenstate radiatively, yielding a normal ordering that aligns with current data. Key advantages include: (i) it elucidates the origin of the neutrino mass hierarchy,; (ii) it successfully explains dark matter; (iii) it preserves the aesthetic of the missing partner mechanism; (iv) it produces a non-zero neutrinoless double beta decay amplitude; and (v) it induces a distinct CP asymmetry, offering a novel source of leptonic CP violation beyond the PMNS matrix.
